Tell me everything: installer@theverge.com. And if you know someone else who might enjoy Installer, forward it to them and tell them to subscribe here.)
The Drop
- The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time. I have a confession to make: I’ve never played this game all the way through. Not sure how! Just missed it. But seeing my friends and coworkers fall back in love with Hyrule has convinced me to get all the way into the remake. I genuinely can’t wait.
- Godzilla Minus Zero. Three years ago, Godzilla Minus One was a big hit and a surprisingly great movie. The sequel came with much higher expectations, but everyone seems to agree it’s a deserving follow-up. I’m not generally one for monster movies, but this series really does it for me.
- Affinity for iPad. Canva’s app now unifies all its tools in one place, just like on the Mac. Affinity makes perfect sense on the iPad, and comes with lots of Apple Pencil integration and clever touch-friendly tools. I’m no designer, but I am excited to play with this as a photo editing tool.
- The Moft Dynamic Folio Case. Here’s one for all you iPhone Duo buyers. Moft’s cases are a little complicated to figure out, but really cleverly designed to make your phone even more useful. I’m guessing this is going to be a lot better than Apple’s weird case / kickstand thing.
- The Peak Design Kickstand Travel Battery. While we’re on the subject of kickstands, here’s the one I’m buying this week. Peak Design makes good stuff, and I frequently find that I need extra juice at exactly the moment I want to watch something on a plane or train. This one’s going right into my backpack and probably never coming out.
- The Bambu Lab H3C. I am dangerously close to becoming a 3D Printer Dude. At $2,500, this one’s a little steep for my wallet, but I think my colleague Sean Hollister is right that this is what the future of 3D printing looks like. Simpler, more foolproof, easy enough even for a goofus like me to make some pretty cool stuff.
- “Ranking the world’s most popular pens for journaling.” I know we all love a good pen — and Peter McKinnon does an excellent job of breaking down a few dozen supposedly good pens to see which ones really hold up. I bought more than one pen after watching this.
- Instagram Edits for Mac. Oh, great, just as I was finally getting good at CapCut! I like the Edits mobile app a lot, and the desktop app seems to be even a little more powerful. Plus: free. This is how I finally take down Cristiano Ronaldo.
- The Sony MDR-3R headphones. Respect to Sony for taking the retro headphone trend all the way to its logical conclusion and just releasing the headphones from the original Walkman. You’ll look a little like Nathan Fielder in You Can See Everything when you wear them, and $60 ain’t cheap, but there’s something so incredibly ’70s-era cool about them.
- The Motorola Signature 27. This is just a pure tour de force of a smartphone spec sheet. Monster camera; brightest screen; giant battery. Also very cool to see a flagship phone with support for GrapheneOS, for the less Google-inclined among us. It’s expensive, and only shipping… someday… but I just like that phones like this exist.
We talked last week about Readwise Books, the new app that’s a mix of Kindle, Goodreads, and Strava. I’m a longtime fan and user of Readwise Reader, so I wasn’t shocked that I liked the new app a lot, too. And I’ve heard from a bunch of you that you do, too!
I’ve talked to Tristan Homsi, one of the Readwise cofounders, a few times over the years, and have always enjoyed hearing his thoughts about reading, apps, and digital products in general. I asked him to share his homescreen to see if I might be able to get a hint about what he’s reading and the other stuff he thinks is good. (I also asked Daniel Doyon, Readwise’s other cofounder, to share, and he didn’t respond. Daniel is dead to me.)
Here’s Tristan’s homescreen, plus some info on the apps he uses and why:
The phone: iPhone 13 (!).Believe it or not, I chose to buy this relatively outdated phone last year… not because it’s my favorite form factor or anything, but because it’s closer in specs to the median device our Readwise users have and helps me build a bit more user empathy with them. I’m able to catch performance regressions and bugs in Readwise that the developers on our team with Duos and Pro Maxes and such miss.
Let me tell you though, iOS 26 itself does not work amazingly on an iPhone 13. Lots of lagging and janky animations. I am somewhat bought into the conspiracy theory that they make the old phones suck so you buy a new one… not so much intentionally, but rather by virtue of just making each successive iOS use more and more resources, doing fancier and fancier things.
The wallpaper: My lovely wife and my cat Sophie :)
The apps: Clock, Settings, Google Calendar, Camera, Google Maps, Spotify, Bay Wheels, Oura, Eight Sleep, Auto Eight, BeReal, ChatGPT, Runmeter, Strava, Readwise Highlights, Readwise Reader, Phone, Messages, Safari.
Of course, I have all three Readwise apps front and center. Highlights and Reader as app icons, and Readwise Books in widget form at the top! It’s a great reminder to jump back into your current book (I’m reading Apple in China right now… speaking of Apple!) instead of scrolling twitter (on a later page), and seeing my friends currently reading really makes me want to jump in and join them :)
I also am a huge fan of the somewhat-defunct social app BeReal. It had its moment in 2022, but quite a few of my friends are still on there! You post once a day, can see what your close friends around the world are doing, and most importantly can’t get sucked in for more than two minutes since it limits you to a random photo or two a day! I still post basically every day, and have almost five years of memories in there.
Speaking of getting sucked in, I don’t have it pictured on my home screen, but I also have Clearspace installed, which helps me stay off of all social media.
Some other apps shown on the homescreen: “auto eight” is something I vibecoded to better control my Eight Sleep mattress (lol)… Strava and Runmeter are awesome for tracking my runs… and Bay Wheels is my main mode of commute around San Francisco daily.
I also asked Tristan to share a few things he’s into right now. Here’s what he sent back:
- I follow some amazing niche internet blogs, which you should check out if you haven’t. I love the blog Slime Mold Time Mold, famous for their citizen science and potato-maxxing. I also love Gwern.net, Deepfates, and Dynomight… among many others!
- And of course I’m always reading books. The most recent fiction series I loved was the Red Knight series — which I can only recommend if you are into dense, dark, fantasy — but man, if you are, the author is a genius.
- For non-fiction, it’s hard for me to plug anything but my favorite book of all time, The Beginning of Infinity. It’s not the easiest to get through, but if you do it will likely change the way you see the world, as it did for me!
Crowdsourced
Here’s what the Installer community is into this week. I want to know what you’re into right now as well! Email installer@theverge.com or message me on Signal — @davidpierce.11 — with your recommendations for anything and everything, and we’ll feature some of our favorites here every week. For even more great recommendations, check out the replies to this post on Threads and this post on Bluesky.
“Finally started reading Dungeon Crawler Carl (recommend); finding the Duo to be a perfect foldable reading device. Going to have to take a break to save Princess Zelda though.” — Will
“I’m playing around with CutWire’s Drift video editor (alt to CapCut) and I’m honestly shocked at how high-quality it feels.” — Kolin
“A wonderful Belgian developer put together an alternative Kobo EPUB reader called Kobalt that I’ve been really enjoying. It’s got a very clean and well-designed UI with a bunch of really nice features that make it a much more enjoyable experience to use. There’s even an Android app, so I also put it on my Supernote Manta to use with larger format content. So much nicer than KOReader!” — Dylan
“As a mourning Arc user, I’ve been on the search for my next browser, especially one with a good mobile experience and this one is AWESOME. Lens Browser feels like what Arc Search on mobile would have become had they stuck with it. Currently only mobile for now, but it does have a Mac toolbar companion for sharing links.” — Garrett
“Since Arc Search is going away, I’ve been using Lens, and it’s exactly what I’ve been wanting in a mobile browser. It’s the perfect Arc Search replacement.” — Corey
“My Boox Picco literally just arrived today. So now I’m trying to churn through Fellowship of the Ring on it, plus my economics textbook.” — Lukas
“I’m trying to get back to the gym, and my motivation is I can only watch a show I want to watch if I’m on the treadmill. I’m finally starting Barry. Turns out, good show!” — Ben
“Well, Zelda..., but also World of Warcraft Forever, but also 007 First Light (which is letting everyone play the opening for free).” — djstarburst
“Playing the Final Fantasy Resonance demo on Switch 2 while waiting for Ocarina of Time to show up at my door and having a blast. It’s not spectacular, but hits the right amount of nostalgia and gameplay for me.” — Micheal
“Been catching up on Avatar: Seven Havens, and oh my goodness, the art style, the characters, the music, the worldbuilding!!!??? It’s all so fresh and delightful and human!” — Olof
Signing off
I’ve mentioned Kagi a bunch of times in this newsletter — it has been my default search engine for the last few years, and I can’t recommend it highly enough. (What if Google, but good, you know?) The challenge with Kagi is it costs $10 a month, which is a lot to ask when Google is free. But as of this week, you can now at least try it for yourself, since Kagi will give you 50 free searches before even asking you to sign up. You get 100 more when you do, even before you pay.
If you search a lot, and miss what Google used to be, give Kagi a whirl. I am a very happy customer, and suspect I will be for a long time.
See you next week!

articles.title: Giá vàng lao dốc, chuyên gia gọi đây là 'cơ hội mua vào của cả đời'
articles.text:
Theo Kitco News, vàng và bạc đã có dấu hiệu phục hồi nhẹ sau phiên bán tháo cuối tuần trước, nhưng đà giảm vẫn rất sâu. Bạc hiện giao dịch thấp hơn khoảng 60% so với mức đỉnh lịch sử 121,64 USD/ounce, trong khi vàng đã chạm mức thấp nhất trong vòng một năm qua.
Nguyên nhân đợt sụt giảm không đến từ các yếu tố cơ bản của kim loại quý. Thay vào đó, nó bắt nguồn từ một hiệu ứng dây chuyền trên thị trường tài chính.
Dù Cục Dự trữ Liên bang Mỹ (Fed) giữ nguyên lãi suất trong cuộc họp gần nhất, nhưng giới đầu tư vẫn kỳ vọng lãi suất sẽ tăng trở lại vào tháng 12. Lãi suất cao làm tăng chi phí cơ hội khi nắm giữ các tài sản không sinh lời như vàng và bạc.
Cùng lúc đó, thị trường chứng khoán Mỹ cũng chao đảo khi chỉ số S&P 500 giảm 2% trong tuần, mức giảm mạnh nhất kể từ đầu tháng 6.
Một số quỹ có thể phải bán các tài sản thanh khoản để bổ sung tiền mặt hoặc đáp ứng yêu cầu ký quỹ, họ không bán những gì họ muốn bán, mà bán những gì dễ bán nhất. Vàng, bạc bị bán ra đầu tiên do tính thanh khoản cao.
‘Đây không phải là khủng hoảng’
Giữa bức tranh ảm đạm đó, bà Jen Bawden, người sáng lập kiêm CEO của công ty đầu tư và tư vấn Bawden Capital có trụ sở tại New York, đã đưa ra một góc nhìn hoàn toàn khác.
Bà Jen Bawden là nhà chiến lược rủi ro kinh tế vĩ mô, đồng thời theo dõi các thị trường vàng, bạc và công nghệ. Theo hồ sơ giới thiệu trên Seeking Alpha và Bawden Capital, bà từng cảnh báo về nguy cơ khủng hoảng tài chính năm 2008 và dự báo giá vàng vượt 1.000 USD/ounce từ năm 2007.
Trong bài bình luận thị trường mới nhất, bà thẳng thắn gọi đợt bán tháo này là “cơ hội mua vào của cuộc đời”.
“Các tiêu đề tin tức tài chính phổ thông đang rầm rộ đưa tin về sự sụp đổ của kim loại quý, khiến các nhà đầu tư cá nhân từng mua vào ở vùng giá cao phải hoảng loạn bán tháo. Với những người thiếu kinh nghiệm, tình cảnh này trông chẳng khác nào một cuộc thảm sát”, bà Bawden nói.
“Nhưng đối với các nhà đầu tư kỳ cựu am hiểu dòng vốn toàn cầu, cơ chế vận hành của thị trường phái sinh và các cú sốc ký quỹ chéo, thì đây không phải là một cuộc khủng hoảng; mà chính là khoảng trống thanh khoản mà chúng ta đã chờ đợi từ lâu”.
Lập luận của bà Bawden tập trung vào áp lực thanh khoản và nhu cầu USD trên thị trường quốc tế. Bà chỉ ra rằng xung đột ở Trung Đông và căng thẳng tại eo biển Hormuz đã đẩy giá dầu Brent vượt mốc 113 USD/thùng.
Theo bà Bawden, giá năng lượng tăng cao và nguy cơ gián đoạn nguồn cung qua eo biển Hormuz làm gia tăng nhu cầu USD của các doanh nghiệp nhập khẩu năng lượng. Khi phải mua thêm USD để thanh toán dầu thô, các nhà nhập khẩu có thể tạo thêm áp lực lên đồng nội tệ, qua đó góp phần hỗ trợ đồng bạc xanh.
USD mạnh lên thường gây bất lợi cho vàng và bạc, vốn được định giá bằng đồng tiền này.
Bài học từ 2008 và 2020
Để củng cố nhận định, bà Bawden viện dẫn các đợt bán tháo trong quá khứ. Bà nhắc lại hai giai đoạn mà giới đầu tư kim loại quý không bao giờ quên: tháng 10/2008 và tháng 3/2020.
Trong cả hai cuộc khủng hoảng đó, vàng và bạc đều bị bán tháo mạnh cùng với thị trường chứng khoán do áp lực thanh khoản.
Theo số liệu được bà Bawden dẫn lại, trong khủng hoảng tài chính năm 2008, vàng từng giảm khoảng 29% và bạc mất hơn 50% so với các mức đỉnh tháng 3 cùng năm. Đến tháng 3/2020, khi đại dịch Covid-19 bùng phát, giá vàng giảm khoảng 10%, còn bạc mất khoảng 35% chỉ trong vài ngày.
Thế nhưng, ngay khi làn sóng bán tháo bắt buộc chấm dứt, giá cả đã quay đầu tăng mạnh. Sau năm 2008, vàng tăng khoảng 170% tính đến tháng 8/2011, còn bạc leo lên gần mức 50 USD/ounce.
Sau tháng 3/2020, vàng tăng khoảng 39% và thiết lập đỉnh cao kỷ lục mới vào tháng 8/2020, trong khi bạc tăng vọt khoảng 150%.
“Khi hoạt động bán tháo bắt buộc chấm dứt, giá các kim loại này đã phục hồi nhanh chóng. Cấu trúc thị trường hiện rất giống với hai giai đoạn đó”, bà Bawden nhận định.
Dù lạc quan về dài hạn nhưng bà Bawden không hề che giấu rủi ro ngắn hạn. Bà thẳng thắn cảnh báo giá vẫn có thể giảm sâu hơn nữa trước khi tạo được vùng đáy bền vững. Nhà đầu tư nên chuẩn bị tâm lý cho kịch bản xấu nhất.
Bản thân vị chuyên gia này cũng đang hành động theo nhận định của mình. Bà cho biết đã đặt sẵn các lệnh chờ mua (limit orders) để tận dụng đà suy yếu tiếp theo, nhắm đến mức chiết khấu từ 20% đến 30% đối với một số cổ phiếu ngành khai thác mỏ được chọn lọc.
Về dài hạn, bà Bawden tin rằng thập kỷ tới sẽ là thời kỳ của các tài sản hữu hình như vàng và bạc.
“Núi nợ công không thể duy trì mãi trong môi trường lãi suất cao mà không gây ảnh hưởng tiêu cực đến ngành ngân hàng và nền kinh tế thực”.
Khi áp lực nợ lên đến điểm tới hạn, các ngân hàng trung ương sẽ buộc phải nới lỏng chính sách, đồng USD suy yếu và dòng vốn toàn cầu sẽ đổ mạnh vào các tài sản thực.

articles.title: Why you don't really need an expensive, high-end router - Engadget
articles.text:
Why you don't really need an expensive, high-end router
You may not be happy with the latest and greatest.
Speed has always been the main selling point for routers. Today's flagship models, like Netgear's Nighthawk RS700S, are rated for up to 19Gbps, come with two 10Gbps ports and eight antennas and sell for more than $500. For most households, that's money spent on a ceiling you'll never touch.
A budget router from a more affordable brand like Netgear or TP-Link, coming in at under $100, will handle the vast majority of what a typical home throws at it. Here's why you don't need a high-end router, and the few cases where spending more makes sense.
Start with the speed coming into your house
A router can't make your internet faster than your plan. The router takes the connection your provider delivers and shares it around your home, and that's the whole job. The FCC's benchmark for what is considered 'broadband' is 100Mbps down and 20Mbps up, so a budget broadband router only has to carry that to your devices without choking.
Before you shop, check what you're paying for. There is no sense in buying a router that transfers more data per second than what is coming in through your wall socket. A router rated far above your plan gives you nothing extra, because the bottleneck is the provider, not the box on your shelf.
What a good budget router actually needs
You don't need a novel-length spec sheet. Four things matter:
Gigabit Ethernet ports
Wired connections are still the most reliable way to hook up a desktop, a console or even a smart TV. Gigabit ports mean the router won't slow down anything plugged into it.
Parental controls
Useful for scheduling screen time and blocking sites on kids' devices. Most decent budget routers include them, often through a free app.
Wi-Fi 6 or better
It's not just about the speed. Wi-Fi 6 is a protocol that handles many devices at once more gracefully than older standards, and that's the real day-to-day improvement: Different devices around the house don't fight for bandwidth.
Whole-home range
Location is just as important as raw speed. A fast router in the wrong corner of the house might provide slow speeds where you actually sit. Match coverage to your space. In a larger home, a mesh kit or a second access point may help more than a pricier single router.
What Wi-Fi 7 adds, and who should get it
Wi-Fi 7 is the newest standard, and it's where most of the expensive routers live. Its headline feature is 320MHz channels in the 6GHz band, which the Wi-Fi Alliance says doubles throughput compared with Wi-Fi 6. This might sound like an enticing proposition, but there's a catch.
To see any of that speed, your devices need Wi-Fi 7 too, and plenty of phones and laptops in people's hands today don't have it. The top speeds quoted on the box are also theoretical maximums, not necessarily what you'll measure in your living room. Wi-Fi 7 routers do work with older devices, but those devices won't get faster just because the router did.
Match the router to your household
The right router depends on who's online. If you live alone or with a roommate, even an older Wi-Fi 5 router can usually handle your phones, laptops and TVs without trouble. In an average household of four to six people, with kids on their iPads, parents on their laptops and grandma gaming in the living room, Wi-Fi 6 is the safer choice because it's built to share the connection among many devices at once.
New, expensive, Wi-Fi 7-enabled routers only start to make sense in a big home or home office with a gigabit-plus fiber plan and plenty of Wi-Fi 7 devices to take advantage of it. If that isn't you, a budget router or a mesh system for a larger space will do the job for far less.
When a high-end router is worth it
In some cases, even a lone user can have a good reason to buy an expensive, high-end router:
Streaming PC VR wirelessly
Meta says Air Link over Wi-Fi works best on the 5GHz band, with the computer wired to the router by Ethernet, and it suggests considering a dedicated router if latency is a problem. A router with plenty of headroom keeps the headset's connection clean when everything else in the house is online.
Moving big files around your home network
Copying video projects to and from a NAS or running regular backups never touches your internet plan, so speeds depend on your own gear instead. Wired is still the best way to do this, but a faster router helps for any device that has to connect over Wi-Fi.
Gaming or live streaming
When a latency spike costs you a match or your viewers, a router with good traffic prioritization and spare capacity helps keep things steady.
A stacked smart home
Cameras, sensors, plugs and speakers add up, and a cheap router can struggle with the sheer number of connections.
If none of that is you, the extra cost buys headroom you won't use.
The short version: what to look for in a router
- Know your plan speed first, and don't pay for a router that outruns it.
- Pick Wi-Fi 6 or better, unless you live alone and have light needs.
- Get gigabit Ethernet ports and parental controls.
- Check that the range suits your space, and consider mesh for bigger homes.
- Don't pay for features your devices can't use yet.
- Spend more only if you stream wireless VR, move large files around your network or game and stream where latency matters.
Do that, and a router under $100 will likely do nearly everything you need.

articles.title: Why a new report on Anthropic automating AI development is alarming researchers
articles.text:
Anthropic is using AI to build more powerful AI. And it appears to be working remarkably well, with the company’s models improving roughly twice as quickly as a year ago, with little indication of slowing down.
Why a new report on Anthropic automating AI development is alarming researchers
AI is dramatically speeding up Anthropic’s research, even as the company calls for slowing down AI development.
That’s according to a new report published Thursday by the AI safety research organization METR, following an 11-week investigation inside the company, as part of a report evaluating its AI research and development. The probe is separate from a program offering safety researchers “employee-like” access to systems in the wake of high-profile hacking incidents over the summer.
The findings offer some of the clearest evidence yet of AI accelerating its own development, raising questions about how quickly the technology could advance toward a future in which AI systems can improve themselves with little or no human involvement. They also come at a pivotal time for Anthropic, which is preparing to go public even as its CEO, Dario Amodei, has publicly called for labs to pump the brakes on AI development.
But while the report offers a rare glimpse into the inner workings of the world’s leading AI labs, what it leaves out is just as revealing. Anthropic was permitted to redact portions of the final report as part of its agreement with METR, and it appears to have exercised that power liberally, raising questions about how much the public really knows about the pace — and risks — of frontier AI development.
Here are some of the biggest takeaways.
AI is dramatically accelerating Anthropic’s research and development
One of METR’s most noteworthy findings is that Anthropic’s AI models are improving roughly twice as quickly as they were a year ago, with benchmark scores suggesting “that Anthropic has made roughly two years of historical progress over the last year.” Crucially, METR’s researchers said they “are confident” that the acceleration was not simply due to scaling up the computing power used to train the models, which historically has been a major driver of AI progress.
Instead, the researchers said that the majority of the acceleration as of October “is due to AI,” with its contribution growing over time. That finding was supported by informal Slack polls and interviews with Anthropic employees, which pointed to sizable productivity gains. METR wrote that employees using Anthropic’s most capable internal model on average self-reported being around 12 times as productive at their respective work as they would have been without AI assistance, around double what staff had reported just a few months earlier while using Mythos 5.
For now, much of that acceleration appears to be coming from AI assisting human researchers, rather than AI working independently, though METR warned that “there are some signs that fully autonomous contributions will play a larger role soon.” Notably, the researchers said they found no clear signs of diminishing returns or observable bottlenecks that could prevent “even faster acceleration.”
Three of Anthropic’s newest AI models remain under wraps
Anthropic’s researchers are using more advanced AI models than the rest of us, with a lot of the acceleration and productivity gains described by METR attributable to unreleased internal models.
Over the past six months, Anthropic has finished training three models it has yet to release, according to METR. The pace of development is swift, with the models — codenamed Model 2, Model 3, and Model 4 — completing training in July, August-September, and September-October, respectively. METR also identified an unreleased model dating back to 2022, called Unreleased 2022. “These are the codenames shared with us; we understand they have different internal codenames,” the researchers wrote.
Anthropic is keeping key information secret
Anthropic gave METR access to a host of non-public information, including confidential research, model performance data, and employee interviews as part of the research process. It had no obligation to do so and by METR’s own admission, the AI lab “shared more information than was initially scoped for this project, surpassing our expectations.” This is commendable, but it is worth noting that Anthropic did not grant researchers unrestricted access, nor the kind of “employee-like” access it has promised other METR safety researchers as part of a separate program announced last month. It is an important distinction, given the reputational benefits companies can gain from independent assessments, even when they come with significant restrictions.
And there were significant restrictions. Anthropic had the power to redact information from METR’s final report — and it used that power extensively. “We submitted a ~100-page full report on our assessment to Anthropic. For the public version, Anthropic redacted a majority of the evidence we found most informative,” METR wrote on X.
METR reiterated those concerns throughout the report, highlighting other limitations on its access. “Our pipeline of information was relatively narrow, and a small number of our requests for data were denied.”
METR repeatedly stressed the impact Anthropic’s redaction decisions had on its ability to communicate its findings and for others to assess what’s going on at the company. It noted that much of the redacted evidence could have “multiple plausible interpretations,” making it difficult for the public to assess its findings, understand the uncertainties surrounding them, and judge the evidence themselves. “As a consequence [of the redactions], the public has to rely on METR’s judgment much more than would be ideal, given the weight of the questions answered here,” the report said.
In the report, METR said Anthropic justified the redactions on the grounds that releasing the information could benefit its rivals. However, METR said “most of the redacted information was very high-level,” even though it said it was not in position to comment whether redactions were justified commercially or not.
“We redacted a lot, and I accept that this makes it harder for others to check METR’s work,” Anthropic cofounder Sam McCandlish acknowledged in a lengthy post on X responding to METR’s findings. “But we determined that sharing exactly what is driving the speedup isn’t the right thing to do, both because it’s commercially sensitive and because it risks handing out a roadmap for others to go faster,” he said, adding that doing so would make the risks METR is concerned about “worse.”
McCandlish said that it’s a trade-off, but maintained Anthropic had made the “right call” in deciding to redact the information. He said the company plans to publish its own report on the speed of AI progress “in the coming weeks,” as well as new steps it’s taking to strengthen safety.
Anthropic is accelerating the very technology it warns is dangerous and faster than many expected
The publication of METR’s report has provoked a fierce backlash among AI safety researchers and commentators, largely centered on an apparent contradiction at the heart of Anthropic’s approach to AI: The company has been one of the most outspoken advocates for safety and responsible development, yet the report suggests it is helping accelerate the technology toward a threshold many consider dangerous, while seemingly failing to live up to its own commitments to transparency and accountability.
For some, the findings suggest that even many of the field’s most aggressive predictions about AI progress may be too conservative. They indicate that recursive self-improvement — AI systems that can autonomously develop increasingly powerful successor systems without human intervention, potentially accelerating development dramatically — may be closer than previously thought, raising concerns about whether existing safety measures can keep pace. While METR’s report only covers Anthropic, OpenAI said in September that it is “making strong progress” toward building an AI researcher that can “further progress on deep learning and alignment” by March 2028.
The report provides evidence about just how quickly AI is accelerating its own development
Marius Hobbhahn, CEO and founder of Apollo Research, which conducts AI safety testing for several leading AI labs, told The Verge the report suggests a pace of AI-enabled research and development even faster than what was forecast in AI 2027, an influential scenario that envisions a key breakthrough toward self-improvement in early 2027. He said the report has attracted so much attention because it provides evidence about something that has been very hard to pin down: Just how quickly AI is accelerating its own development.
Hobbhahn said the findings were broadly in line with what many in the field had expected, perhaps a little faster. Alan Chan, a senior research fellow at tech policy research center GovAI, told The Verge that the findings should prompt skeptics to reconsider their stance on AI accelerating AI development, and possibly shorten their timelines to when we will have systems that can fully automate tasks like software engineering.
On X, other researchers commented on the rate of acceleration and its implications for AI development. Sydney Von Arx, founder and CEO of AI safety organization The Nightingale Collective and a former METR researcher, also compared the findings to AI 2027’s timeline. Ryan Greenblatt, a METR researcher formerly of AI safety organization Redwood Research and one of three external researchers permitted to investigate OpenAI’s hack of Hugging Face, said he “was seriously wrong about RSI speed up; I previously expected much less in 2026.”
Frustration is mounting over Anthropic’s approach to safety
Beyond highlighting the speed of AI development, the report has also fueled a growing sense of frustration over Anthropic’s role in driving that progress. The company has been one of the most vocal proponents of responsible AI development — and no stranger to calling for others to slow down — yet appears to be racing ahead itself. This report only builds on already heightened tensions from its IPO prospectus and future plans released last month.
Anthropic’s decision to heavily redact the report, citing grounds that revealing more could help its rivals accelerate their own development, has fueled accusations of hypocrisy. Daniel Kokotajlo, a former OpenAI researcher who now runs the AI Futures Project, which published AI 2027, accused Anthropic of “recklessly gambling with our lives,” adding that “it is pretty rich” of the company to cite others going faster as a reason to redact information when it does “not appear to be slowing down much at all.”
Anthropic declined to answer The Verge’s questions about the report and ensuing criticism, instead directing us to McCandlish’s post.
The redactions have also renewed calls for greater transparency and independent oversight of frontier AI labs, which grew to new heights earlier this year following a spate of incidents involving rogue AI agents. Brianna Rosen, research director for frontier security at the Institute for AI Policy and Strategy, told The Verge that it was concerning that companies, not governments, were effectively calling the shots on automating AI research. “For democratic oversight to work, independent evaluators need the freedom to explain why they reached their conclusions, governments need to assess the evidence themselves, and the public has to trust this process,” Rosen said. “The report was not sufficiently transparent about the evidence.”
Pressure is building for more transparency from AI labs
Hobbhahn echoed Rosen’s concerns, saying that much of the reaction to the report stems from the apparent gap between Anthropic’s public safety stance and its actions. He pointed to the company’s decision to cancel part of the assessment designed to evaluate how much compute it allocates to safety work versus improving capabilities. METR said the company said “this was due to wanting to keep the engagement focused on risk assessment for the time being, and that it would revisit compute allocation verification later on.”
For Hobbhahn, the episode underscores the need for independent safety researchers to be embedded more deeply within AI labs, with significant access to internal systems and evidence. While his organization stands to benefit from such arrangements — Apollo is taking steps toward becoming an embedded evaluator at frontier labs — he is far from alone in calling for stronger oversight of AI development.
Others have called for more direct action. In a direct response to the report, New York state Assemblyman Alex Bores, a key figure shaping the Democrats’ AI agenda, called on Congress to “ban RSI, this year if possible.” With the blue wave of Democrats — many of whom campaigned against AI companies — taking office soon, the prospect of tougher restrictions is a very real possibility.
And with AI research showing little sign of slowing down, the pressure is set to intensify. Hobbhahn said he had another takeaway from the report, too: “Brace for craziness,” he said. “It is going to go very fast,” likely way too fast for society or politics to keep up.

articles.title: The accessory Samsung Galaxy S26 users should be taking advantage of - Engadget
articles.text:
The accessory Samsung Galaxy S26 users should be taking advantage of
It's not exciting, but it sure is useful.
The Samsung Galaxy S26 series is the Korean giant's current flagship, and it's no surprise they've been well received. Samsung's decades of iteration mean modern users get sleek software running on well-optimized hardware, with little trace of the growing pains users saw in the early days of Galaxy products.
But that longevity has bred complacency, and we've seen multiple generations of Galaxy S devices without meaningful upgrades to the camera or battery. That's why one Galaxy S26 upgrade in particular stood out to observers at launch: Better charging speeds on the top-end Galaxy S26 Ultra and a bigger battery on the base S26.
For years, Samsung's top-tier phones were stuck at 45-watt charging, even as Chinese manufacturers started offering truly ludicrous charging speeds of 80 watts and higher. There are good reasons not to mess with battery tech, especially if you're Samsung, but it was getting a bit embarrassing. That's changed with the S26 Ultra, which is the first Samsung Galaxy capable of charging at up to 60 watts. Wireless charging is faster on the S26 Ultra and S26+, too. While battery capacities remain the same, faster charging means fewer worries about daily longevity.
The base S26 didn't get any charging upgrades — it remains stuck at 25 watts — but received a bigger battery, going from 4,000 mAh in the S25 to 4,300. So, if you're rocking a Galaxy S26, especially the Ultra, the one accessory you should take advantage of is one Samsung no longer includes in the box: a charger.
The S26 Ultra got a massive charging upgrade, but the charger isn't included
For several years, Samsung has followed Apple's lead by not including charging bricks with new Galaxy devices. Unbox a new S26 Ultra and, aside from an aging USB 2.0 cable, you'll get no accessories included with your $1,400 smartphone. While charging bricks can indeed contribute heavily to e-waste, most people are unlikely to have a 60-watt charger lying around. That means most people using a pre-owned charger for their Galaxy S26 Ultra likely aren't benefiting from the phone's improved charging.
At full speed, which Samsung calls Super Fast Charging 3.0, the S26 Ultra can charge from dead to around 75 percent in just half an hour. That's quick enough to top up a low battery before you leave work and still have enough juice for the commute home. The last charger Samsung shipped with a phone was a 25-watt brick included with the S20 Ultra in 2020. Even that was underpowered for that phone's 45-watt charging. If you're still using that charger for your S26 Ultra, you've been missing out.
Thankfully, third-party chargers have improved significantly and stayed affordable. Today, some of the best fast chargers in 2026 deliver 100 watts or more and charge multiple devices, all while fitting into nearly any pocket or bag. Top brands like Anker, Belkin, and Ugreen make chargers using gallium nitride (GaN), which offers more efficient power delivery in a smaller form factor. Sixty-watt chargers can be had for around $40, and even those with twice the power are still very affordable.
Don't neglect improved wireless charging speeds on your Galaxy S26+ and S26 Ultra
Wired charging will always be faster than wireless (unless we figure out how to overcome some pretty ironclad laws of thermodynamics), but that doesn't mean both aren't improving. The Galaxy S26+ got a bump to 20-watt wireless charging, while the S26 Ultra now charges wirelessly at 25 watts. That latter figure is the top speed of current-generation Qi2.2 wireless charging.
To take advantage of those speeds, you need two accessories. Because high-speed wireless charging requires MagSafe-style Qi2 magnetic alignment, and since Samsung once again declined to build those magnets into the phones, you'll need a 25-watt wireless charging pad and a magnetic case to go along with it. It's easy to find a good charging pad; any magnetic wireless charger rated for 25 watts from a reputable brand will do. But cases are more complicated.
A case is actually the last thing you want between your phone and a wireless charger, as the thicker the case is, the less efficient the charging. Thus, when choosing a case, check how thick it is inside the magnetic charging ring. Case material also matters: you want one without metal components, as they can cause charging issues. Finally, it's also a good idea to check professional and user reviews to see whether anyone has had wireless charging issues.

articles.title: What's the point of buying a touchscreen laptop when you could just get a tablet? - Engadget
articles.text:
What's the point of buying a touchscreen laptop when you could just get a tablet?
A touchscreen laptop gives you more options, but it's a secondary benefit to everything else a laptop offers.
Recently, Apple made headlines by announcing its first-ever touchscreen Mac, the PROLED MacBook Pro. That's despite co-founder Steve Jobs famously decrying touchscreen laptops as "ergonomically terrible," and launching an alternative in the form of 2010's iPad. In fact, iPads have become increasingly Mac-like in recent years, with many models adopting the same processors and iPadOS getting a similar multitasking interface. Some Android tablets have becoming increasingly PC-like, too.
Dedicated tablets do have advantages over laptops. They're often hundreds of dollars cheaper, which matters when memory prices are rocketing out of control. And of course, they're lighter and more portable, which can make them a godsend if you want to get tasks done (or just watch a few movies) on a long flight.
However, there are still reasons to buy a touchscreen laptop, even if you're not going to splurge on a device as costly as a MacBook Pro. It's mostly a combination of deeper functionality and what's included with that (normally) higher upfront cost.
How (touchscreen) laptops often win over pure tablets
All laptops incorporate a keyboard and trackpad, whereas those are paid add-ons for tablets. You may not need either, depending on your goals. But if nothing else, a physical keyboard is far easier to type on than a touchscreen, owing to its ergonomic positioning and feedback. It also gives you back a large amount of screen space. A trackpad improves precision for functions like selecting text or manipulating timelines in audio and video editors.
Tablets also tend to skimp on ports, with iPads being one of the worst offenders with their single port. You might get two with some other brands. For some productivity purposes, you may then end up having to buy a USB hub or Thunderbolt dock, which can actually make a tablet feel less portable than a comparable laptop unless you're able to able to leave your accessories behind most of the time.
The real killers tend to be software and horsepower. Most tablets run either Android or iPadOS, which are really locked-down smartphone operating systems at their core. Laptops running Windows, macOS or Linux have fewer barriers, giving them access to more capable apps that sometimes have no real Android or iPad equivalent. Meanwhile, more expensive laptops can feature advanced GPUs that wipe the floor with what's possible on even an iPad Pro. Professionals and hardcore gamers who need a heavy-duty device have little choice but a laptop for the software they want.
You might have noticed that this discussion didn't talk much about the specific benefits of a touchscreen on a laptop, which is because they're mostly secondary supports to a laptop's pros. They can make some tasks you do on your laptop a bit more convenient, like scrolling through long pages with your finger or more naturally testing mobile apps you're developing, but are hardly a selling point on their own.
Foldable 2-in-1 laptops can pull double duty as your work device and a tablet for scrolling through social media on the couch, but Windows and macOS aren't built around touch like Android and iPadOS. Extended note-taking or drawing on a vertical touchscreen are not comfortable, so you're better off with a drawing pad or tablet for those.
The real question you should be asking
It's certainly possible to get by with a tablet. You might prefer one not just for price and portability, but the intuitive touch-centric workflow that matches your phone. It's why I sometimes recommend an iPad as a first computer for both kids and seniors. But the more advanced your needs, the more likely a tablet is to fall short, especially if you're not willing to spend a few hundred dollars on an iPad case with an attached keyboard and trackpad or a separate keyboard and mouse combo.
Ultimately, you should ask yourself whether you need a touchscreen device at all. Touch tech is rarely essential unless you're doing illustration, handwritten notes or high-end photo editing. A touchless laptop might cost as much as an equivalent tablet, or let you put the savings towards upgrades like a better GPU or a bigger screen.
And we can't forget about coping with those extreme memory prices. Putting cash aside for the right amount of RAM could enable smoother multitasking, while doing the same for storage could mean having to juggle and delete files and apps less often. Those are upgrades you can appreciate for the life of the device, compared to a touchscreen you might not have a real use for after a few weeks.

articles.title: Trump targets Slotkin in call for DOJ probe of alleged Democratic threats to Republicans
articles.text:
President Donald Trump said Saturday that he was ordering the Justice Department to investigate Democratic leaders over what he described as threats against Republican officials, donors and supporters, without identifying the alleged communications or providing evidence of criminal conduct.
"The Democrats are going around threatening a lot of people, including the Attorney General of the United States, and others, with Impeachment and many other forms of punishment, even though they admit they have no reason to do so," Trump said in a Truth Social post.
The alleged threats, the president said, are "extortion at the highest level," he wrote. "I am ordering the Department of Justice to look into this criminal act, immediately!"
In his post, Trump claimed that Democratic Sen. Elissa Slotkin of Michigan is planning to "go after all young people that believe in Republican Values."
Trump was apparently referencing a speech Slotkin made at a University of Chicago event on Oct. 13. At the time, Slotkin said: "I want young people coming out of school to say, 'Should I go work for the Trump administration?'...I want them to be like, 'Lord, that might be buying myself a ton of problems that I don't want. And so let me avoid participating in that.' I want that deterrence message sent."
Slotkin alleges that she, her family and her staff faced physical and legal intimidation after the posting of a November 2025 video in which Slotkin and other Democratic leaders called on the U.S. military to "refuse illegal orders" following the airstrikes targeting boats in the Caribbean.
On Nov. 20, Trump called the video treason and said "an example must be set."
The FBI contacted lawmakers, including Slotkin, days later. In February, Slotkin declined to sit for an interview the Justice Department requested about the video.
"The intimidation is the point, and I'm not gonna go along with that," the senator said in February. A federal grand jury later declined to indict the video participants.
Now, Trump alleges Democrats are threatening legal intimidation against Republican leaders and their supporters.
"Republicans should get smart, fast! Threatening letters have been sent to many people, all innocent, from Democrat Political Leaders," the president wrote.
The White House and Slotkin didn't immediately respond to a request for comment.

articles.title: Trump offers UFC chief Dana White press secretary job
articles.text:
President Donald Trump offered UFC president and CEO Dana White the job of press secretary on Saturday.
In a post on Truth Social, Trump said: "I am pleased to announce that the Great Dana White, a violent Fighter and Warrior, has been offered the job of Press Secretary of the United States."
"We need these people to defend us against the Lunatic Left," Trump wrote. "Dana will be a Press Secretary like none other. Dana, please take the job!"
CNN, citing a source, reported White had declined the president's offer.
Earlier Saturday, White posted a picture of himself on Instagram stories standing behind the press secretary's lectern in the White House, with the caption, "On to the next chapter."
It was unclear whether White had accepted the position or was simply acknowledging the president's request as a joke.
Trump said that he was offering White the job of "Press Secretary of the United States," but the president's spokesperson is called the "White House press secretary." Trump also recently speculated about considering Trump loyalist and rapper Nicki Minaj as press secretary, in an interview with podcaster Benny Johnson.
Trump said the job offer to White extended to his assistants, "even though some are not from our Country." The so-called assistants Trump named included current and former UFC mixed martial arts fighters from countries such as Brazil and Russia.
In October, White House press secretary Katie Zacharia left the position just five days after her stint as Karoline Leavitt's replacement began.
The president told reporters he suggested Zacharia quit after her first and only press briefing, where, in her six minutes answering questions behind the lectern, she only took questions from three conservative outlets.
"I just spoke to her about it. I said, 'Katie, is this for you?'" Trump said outside the White House on Oct. 16.
The president's appeal to White follows Friday's announcement that Trump's deputy chief of staff, Stephen Miller, would be promoted to chief of staff, replacing Susie Wiles.
Trump's stunning shake-up came just three days after Democrats won a landslide victory in the midterm elections, gaining majority control in the House and Senate.
The president and White have a longstanding friendship. During Trump's first campaign in 2016, White praised the then-Republican nominee and called him a "fighter."
"Nobody took us seriously. Nobody. Except Donald Trump. Donald was the first guy to recognize the potential we saw in the UFC and encouraged us to build our business," White said.
And for his 80th birthday in June, President Trump hosted a UFC match — dubbed UFC Freedom 250 — on the White House's South Lawn.
The White House and the UFC didn't immediately respond to a request for comment.
— CNBC's Kevin Breuninger contributed to this report.
CORRECTION: This article has been updated to correct the spelling of Karoline Leavitt's name.

articles.title: Meta chief strategy officer Dave Wehner leaves to join AI infrastructure startup Fireworks as CFO
articles.text:
Dave Wehner, Meta's chief strategy officer, is leaving the company for four-year-old AI startup Fireworks.
At Fireworks — an AI inference and model-training platform focused on open models that was valued at $17.5 billion during a Series D fundraising round in July — Wehner will assume the CFO role, he announced on X on Friday.
Wehner will be tasked with scaling the company's finances and operations, Fireworks CEO Lin Qiao said in a statement to CNBC.
"Fireworks has the right mission for the moment," Wehner wrote on X, adding: "I've become increasingly bullish on what they are building. There's a remarkable depth of technical talent here, coupled with a very practical focus on what customers need."
The AI startup, founded in 2022 by former Meta and Google employees, is a platform that lets developers customize and run open models for their businesses. Its latest investment round was led by Atreides Management, Index Ventures and TCV, but Fireworks is also backed by Nvidia and Sequoia Capital. Business Insider reported that it is in early talks to raise funds again at a possible $30 billion to $40 billion valuation.
Wehner joined Meta, then called Facebook, in 2012 and was the company's chief financial officer from 2014 to 2022.
"Dave helped guide Meta through tremendous growth and complexity over 14 years, and brought disciplined thinking to some of our hardest company-level decisions," Meta COO Javier Olivan said in a statement to CNBC.
Fireworks is notably smaller than Meta — the tech giant has about a $1.56 trillion market capitalization as of Friday's close — and its competitors, which include OpenAI and Anthropic.
"Dave told me he wanted to get back to a smaller company where he could build toward a big impact again," Fireworks' Lin wrote in a LinkedIn post on Friday. "He sees AI as the defining technology shift of his lifetime and wants to help shape what comes next."
The company's size has not made it immune to the risks and complications often associated with AI technology. In October, the company found "a security incident involving unauthorized use of internal Fireworks credentials," in which "an unauthorized third party accessed environment variables used in evaluation jobs in a limited number of customer accounts," it said in a press release.
"Based on our investigation at this time, we have not detected evidence of unauthorized access to customer models, datasets, training data, personal information, or inference traffic within the Fireworks security perimeter or control," the release said.

articles.title: Decisive election. Dramatic stock swings. How we handled the market last week
articles.text: What a week on Wall Street. The market breathed a sigh of relief after the midterms, following a couple of up-and-down sessions to start the week. Buyers came out of the woodwork Wednesday — not necessarily because of any one outcome but because the voting was over. The Dow surged 3%, while the S & P 500 and Nasdaq each rose about half as much, reflecting broad appetite for stocks. The idea that a Democratic wave might slow the data center buildout simmered beneath the surface, pressuring key pockets of the AI trade. Jim Cramer cautioned that the first-day reaction to Tuesday's election, which saw Democrats flip both the House and the Senate, along with a handful of swing-state gubernatorial races, might be overly optimistic. Then, Thursday happened. Jim's warning that the prior day's rally might not accurately reflect how investors felt proved prophetic. The Dow, S & P 500, and Nasdaq had their worst single sessions since April 2025. The Nasdaq plunged 5.5% into correction territory — defined as a drop of at least 10% from recent highs. The tech-heavy index's record high was just over a month ago. The tech selling, however, was not completely out of the blue. The AI trade had been wavering for weeks as concerns mounted about the extraordinary levels of borrowing to bring more computing capacity online. The Nasdaq saw a few nasty sell-off days in the run-up to the election. Along the way, the more defensive parts of the market, from healthcare to consumer staples, were moving higher. There were few places to hide in Thursday's market. The buildout stocks were the epicenter of selling again, on fears that if fewer data centers come online in future years, the projected earnings for chipmakers and power companies are too lofty, and the stocks aren't actually getting cheaper as they decline. Micron lost more than 17% on the session, while Intel and Nvidia lost over 10% and 9%, respectively. (The three stocks were also our worst performers for the week). One stock that finished the day in the green was Cardinal Health , which reported an impressive quarter before the bell. We used that strength to book big profits and pad our cash position. We also trimmed Eli Lilly . As Jim always says, you can't just sell losers. We still love both those stocks. (Cardinal Health was up 8.5% for the week and was our best performer.) Down but not out, the market made a stand Friday. While the Dow was modestly lower, the S & P 500 and Nasdaq staged decent bounce-back rallies. Like Wednesday, a note of caution about whether Friday's tech buying is for real is warranted. When it was all said and done, the Dow lost 1% last week, while the S & P 500 and Nasdaq sank 2.7% and 3.4%, respectively. Unfortunately, November has picked right up where October left off, with tech slumping and the defensive parts of the market on the upswing. With the dust settling from this up-and-down week, two things are becoming clearer. First, not every AI-related company would be hurt equally if the data center buildout slows down. The neoclouds, like CoreWeave , that need financing to grow are the most vulnerable. The established hyperscalers, including Club names Amazon , Alphabet , and Microsoft , might not grow as much if the AI boom cools off, but they are still in the pole positions because of their massive scale. They could also rein in spending, which many investors would welcome. The demand for compute, as we have learned time and again this earnings season, remains off the charts. Second, as Jim has said repeatedly, this market underscores why owning a diversified portfolio is such an important strategy for staying in the game. So, against that backdrop, what have we been doing to protect our gains and pivot the portfolio to the new realities? On Friday, Jim held the CNBC Investing Club's 4th Annual Meeting to communicate his strategy. Put simply, he said he wants to continue to lighten up on data center and lean into non-AI. "I want to circle the wagons around the best and redeploy capital into other, less risky stocks, continuing my paring, going for the best and taking losses if we have to, to get to higher ground." He shared the stage at the New York Stock Exchange with portfolio director Jeff Marks. They updated their views on every name in the portfolio and mentioned two stocks to buy: FedEx and Kimberly-Clark . We bought more of these about a month ago. In addition to those Cardinal and Lilly trades, we were actively trading last week to get bigger in non-tech (added to Boeing and Goldman Sachs ) and to beef up our cash position (also trimmed DuPont , twice). With more than 15% of the Club portfolio in cash, Jim said at the Annual Meeting, we have ample dry powder. But, uncharacteristically, he added, "It's not burning a hole in my pocket." (See here for a full list of the stocks in Jim Cramer's Charitable Trust.) As a subscriber to the CNBC Investing Club with Jim Cramer, you will receive a trade alert before Jim makes a trade. Jim waits 45 minutes after sending a trade alert before buying or selling a stock in his charitable trust's portfolio. If Jim has talked about a stock on CNBC TV, he waits 72 hours after issuing the trade alert before executing the trade. articles.title: Why the prognosis for healthcare stocks is uncertain ahead of Congress’ new makeup
articles.text:
Healthcare stocks may struggle to gain momentum as Democrats prepare to take over Congress.
Jared Holz, who covers healthcare for Mizuho, says the outlook for the sector is uncertain because of likely gridlock between lawmakers.
"The next couple of years I really can't see too much happening," the firm's sector specialist told CNBC's "Fast Money" on Wednesday. "I'm not sure you want to own everything, but you can pick and choose the names… Pharma is trading more expensive than tech for the first time in 20 years. So, I backed away from pharma. I would look at medtech."
The State Street Health Care Select ETF (XLV) jumped 3% a day after Election Day.
"You had this very weird situation where typically you wouldn't have all of these categories work in tandem, and they did. So, I think some things just a little bit off," said Holz, a day before healthcare got swept up in Thursday's Wall Street sell-off.
According to Holz, healthcare's real booster shot may come if a Democrat wins the White House in 2028.
"Then I think you see some of the Trump strategies rolled back. That's where I think healthcare could actually perform well," said Holz, who added it hinges on Democrats retaining the Senate and House.
For investors who are long on healthcare, Holz said each subsector should be treated differently.
"Can we get some of the regulation that has taken place over the past couple of years and overturn that over the near term? I don't necessarily believe so," Holz said. "But if you do, then you probably want to be long some of these medical device stocks that are at or near multi-year lows."
The State Street Health Care Select ETF ended virtually flat this week. It's up around 32% since President Trump took office in January 2025 — beating the S&P 500 by almost 9 percentage points.

articles.title: America's newest small business owners with no employees are off to a hot start in AI era
articles.text:
It takes hundreds of billions of dollars for the tech giants to scale artificial intelligence, but it takes just a few AI tools for the smallest companies in the U.S. economy to get up and running with a cost-competitive business model.
Alex Willen expects the 12 e-commerce brands he operates with no employees to generate between $2.5 million and $3 million this year. Kristin Ginn left Microsoft in March and started trnsfrmAItn, an AI-adoption consultancy. Seven months later, she has roughly $250,000 in business received or contracted through year-end with no employees or regular contractors.
"The biggest misconception is that it's just about individual productivity; it's actually about leveraging AI to perform tasks that previously required a whole team," said Stanford economist Erik Brynjolfsson.
Early research on the impact of AI within the solopreneur business world bears watching.
According to Liya Palagashvili, a labor economist and director of the Labor Policy Project at George Mason University's Mercatus Center, new business formation is rising in direct correlation to applications unlikely to become employer firms.
In industries highly exposed to AI, business applications without early signs of hiring rose 26.8% from the first quarter of 2024 through the first quarter of 2026, from roughly 222,000 to 281,000 per quarter.
Over the same period, applications in those industries with stronger indications of eventually becoming employer businesses fell 6.4%. In construction and wholesale trade, which Palagashvili used as a comparison group, non-employer-type applications declined 0.4%.
"What AI is doing is giving those capabilities directly into the hands of the individual," she said.
Palagashvili cautioned that the findings are preliminary and descriptive and do not establish that AI caused the increase. The Census-based measure identifies applications without indicators associated with near-term payroll or hiring plans; it does not show that those businesses ultimately remained one-person firms or never hired employees.
But Willen shows what the economics can look like.
Anthropic's Claude helps with bookkeeping, customer service, advertising, and inventory across his businesses, while OpenAI image tools perform work that once went to photographers and designers.
Without AI, Willen said, "I'd probably need one other full-time person, plus I'd need to use contractors for photography, design, bookkeeping, and ad management."
A traditional product photography shoot could cost $2,000 to $5,000, and a designer $300 to $1,000 for new listing images, he said.
When AI directly eliminates one of those expenses, Willen said, "that money just goes into my pocket."
AI has also allowed him to pursue revenue channels he would not have previously considered. After acquiring Lone Trail, a hunting-gear brand selling binocular harnesses, packs, and other outdoor accessories, Willen said its Shopify site accounted for roughly 1% of sales. Rather than shut down the channel, he used ChatGPT and Claude to rebuild the site and AI to help run Meta advertising. In a recent 30-day period, he said, Shopify accounted for roughly 30% of Lone Trail's revenue.
"That's going to end up being at least six figures of annual revenue that would not exist without AI," Willen said.
Ginn's business shows how quickly a new entrant can reach meaningful revenue without first building an organization around it. She uses AI to help with proposals, pricing, strategy, and other work and is exploring an AI agent to perform part of a labor-intensive client process.
A survey conducted by accounting and invoicing software company FreshBooks identified similar behavior more broadly. Seventy-nine percent of solopreneurs said they had tried AI before hiring someone for a task they could not perform themselves (the same figure was 86% among when including microbusiness owners). AI allows them to "look much bigger than they are," FreshBooks CEO Shaheen Javadizadeh said.
But among existing small businesses, the available data tells another story. Gusto, a payroll and HR software company that serves small businesses, tracked businesses after they adopted AI and found their headcount was about 7% higher after a year than a comparable businesses that knew about AI but had not adopted it. Among firms with fewer than 10 employees, AI adopters grew headcount about 10% more than comparable non-adopters.
Willen's experience also highlights a tradeoff in the new business model: operating with fewer people does not eliminate reliance on larger technology platforms. Roughly 80% of its overall revenue still comes through Amazon, and he uses Meta and Shopify to expand direct sales. Ginn has no staff, but LinkedIn has been one of the biggest drivers of customers to her consultancy, she said.
Brynjolfsson said the proliferation of smaller producers can actually increase the value of the platforms that connect them with the buyers.
"There's this long tail of products, but at the same time, big platforms like Amazon are more powerful than ever because they aggregate all of these and they bring them together," Brynjolfsson said.
But the relationship is not as simple as labor savings flowing directly to Big Tech. Willen said some of the money he saves becomes profit, while Ginn spends less than $60 a month on paid AI tools.
AI can make it economical for more small producers to exist. And as core business production becomes cheaper, small businesses place greater focus on customer acquisition and distribution, Brynjolfsson said.
Brynjolfsson believes that while solopreneurs will thrive, use of AI will at the same time lead to the creation of even larger firms, on average, than exist today.
In a September research report titled "AI's Use of Knowledge in Society," Brynjolfsson and Zoë Hitzig, a researcher at the Anthropic Institute who studies the social and economic impacts of AI, argue that as AI codifies knowledge previously scattered among workers and enables more information to be aggregated and acted upon centrally, firms will grow larger on average, while industry concentration increases and local managerial autonomy declines. The researchers say early evidence is largely consistent with those patterns.
That's bad news for medium-sized companies. Brynjolfsson predicts AI could contribute to a "hollowing out" of midsize firms — very small teams capable of doing more at one end and giant organizations exploiting AI and scale at the other.
"The fat in the middle — the layers of management focused on internal coordination — will likely be significantly reduced," he said.
Adam Branch has experienced a version of that shift from inside two very different technology companies.
Before founding rhino.ai, an enterprise software company that uses AI to modernize legacy systems, Branch built Incentive Technology Group, a traditional technology services company that grew to roughly 500 employees. Under that model, winning more work meant hiring more people, he said.
"With rhino.ai, we're building AI software to do more of the work those teams used to do," said Branch.
Rhino.ai has roughly 50 employees. Branch estimates comparable modernization work can now be performed with three to four times the productivity per employee.
His team estimates labor represented roughly 85% of operating spending at ITG, and technology about 5%. At rhino.ai, Branch puts labor at roughly 40%, while technology, including cloud, software, and AI models, represents about 25%.
AWS sees a similar loosening of the relationship between revenue and headcount among AI-native startups. Its Engines of Growth research, an independent global study of 3,413 startup founders and senior leaders across 20 countries, found those companies grew revenue an average 156% annually versus 65% for startups overall, while more than half generated over $400,000 in revenue per employee. The report focused on companies under five years old that use AI in its most advanced forms.
"Growth used to be tied directly to how many people you could hire," said Ruba Borno, vice president of AWS Specialists and Partners. "Now founders can scale with technology, not just headcount."
Brynjolfsson does not see the result as simply Big Tech winning at everyone else's expense. Entrepreneurs can keep some of the productivity gains, consumers get more choice, and platforms benefit from supplying the technology and connecting more producers with customers, he said.
"The platforms and the people who are creating the tools are winning because they are able to sell them, the solopreneurs are winning because they are able to use them, and the consumers are winning because they are getting new products that they didn't get before," he said. "It's mostly a bigger pie, so it's a win-win-win — a triple win."
What AI may change is the shape of that bigger pie, he said.
"Whenever there's a technology change, a platform change, obviously it benefits the companies that are creating those platforms and technologies," Brynjolfsson said. "But it also benefits new entrants who can start fresh."

articles.title: Many workers lose unused FSA money — but could still come out ahead. Here's how
articles.text:
Health flexible spending accounts, or FSAs, are tax-advantaged accounts that let workers set aside pretax money to cover eligible health expenses. However, they're often use it or lose it, with unspent balances forfeited at the end of the plan year.
About 4 in 10 workers with health FSAs forfeited unused money in 2024, according to an October report from the Employee Benefit Research Institute, a nonprofit research organization. Among those FSA account holders, the average forfeiture was $404, down from $436 in 2023. The research examined more than 3.3 million accounts representing $3.9 billion in contributions.
Yet even workers who don't zero out their balance may still benefit from using an FSA, compared with what they would have spent using after-tax dollars to cover the same expenses.
"Even if someone forfeits FSA funds back to their employer, they can still come out ahead — relative to not participating in an FSA — if the amount they forfeited is less than the tax savings they realized," said Jake Spiegel, a senior research associate for EBRI and author of the study.
One-third of FSA holders face use it or lose it
Nearly three-quarters — 72% — of state and local government workers and 47% of private-sector workers have access to a health FSA in 2026, according to the Bureau of Labor Statistics. That compares with 68% and 40%, respectively, in 2017.
FSAs differ from health savings accounts, or HSAs, which some people use in conjunction with high-deductible health plans. Although both let you set aside pretax money for health care expenses, HSAs let you roll over your balance from year to year, and even invest it.
Roughly a third of FSA users in the EBRI database face a strict use-it-or-lose-it provision, Spiegel said. The rest either are permitted by their employers to carry over an amount — up to $680 in 2026 — into the following year or are offered a grace period of up to 2.5 months after the deadline to incur additional expenses or face forfeiture. However, employers cannot offer both options.
While many plans have a Dec. 31 deadline for spending FSA money, some employers have deadlines falling in other parts of the year, said Rachel Rouleau, chief compliance officer for Health-E Commerce, parent company of online retailers FSA Store and HSA Store.
"Understanding these plan-specific deadlines is essential, so employees should check with their employer or FSA administrator to avoid forfeiting unused funds," Rouleau said.
Additionally, many employers give you extra time — typically three months after the deadline — to submit receipts for qualifying expenses that occurred during the previous plan year.
How to calculate your financial benefit
For 2026, the maximum contribution allowed to health FSAs is $3,400. In 2027, that amount will be $3,500, the IRS announced Thursday.
Part of the reason workers have forfeitures may be that they must decide how much they want to contribute to their FSA before the plan year begins.
"It's difficult to project how much you'll need to spend on health care, especially if you are particularly healthy and don't have a chronic condition with predictable prescription drug costs," Spiegel said.
Contributions to FSAs are withheld from paychecks and generally avoid federal taxes, as well as so-called payroll taxes — known as FICA — that go toward Social Security and Medicare. They also may avoid state and local taxes, depending on where you live.
To determine how much you're saving in taxes by using an FSA, you can add up those tax rates and apply the total to your contribution, said certified financial planner Sean Lovison, founder of Purpose Built Financial Services in Moorestown, New Jersey.
For example, say that your federal, FICA, state and local taxes total 35% and you contributed the maximum allowed — $3,400 for 2026. In this case, the calculation would result in $1,190 in estimated tax savings, which is "how much you're saving on taxes by contributing to your FSA," Lovison said.
The illustration assumes the worker receives no employer contribution to the FSA and the tax rate applies to the entire contribution.
As long as the number you're forfeiting from your FSA is less than [your tax savings], you're going to come out ahead.Sean LovisonFounder of Purpose Built Financial Services
"As long as the number you're forfeiting from your FSA is less than that number, you're going to come out ahead," Lovison said.
Of course, he said, "you don't want to walk away from FSA money, but at the same time, from a mathematical standpoint, you're still coming out ahead."
If you face a forfeiture, you can use it to help inform your decision on how much to put toward your FSA for 2027, if you haven't already made benefit elections for next year.
"Employees should look at their anticipated healthcare expenses over the coming year and consider both their daily health routines and expected annual expenses," Rouleau said. "This includes recurring prescriptions, doctor visits, copays, deductibles, dental and vision care, and other eligible out-of-pocket healthcare expenses for themselves and their eligible dependents."
'Thousands' of ways to spend unused balance
Before you resign yourself to a forfeiture, keep in mind that there are also many ways to use the money on eligible expenses before the end of the year.
"There are thousands of ways consumers can responsibly spend down their FSA dollars, from everyday healthcare essentials to eligible telehealth services," Rouleau said.
Additionally, "many consumers are surprised to learn that a wide range of over-the-counter medications, menstrual care products, sunscreen, first-aid supplies and certain health-monitoring devices are FSA-eligible," Rouleau said.
That's in addition to doctor and dentist appointments, prescription drugs and other healthcare services such as acupuncture and addiction treatment, according to the IRS.
If you're unsure whether you have money remaining in your FSA or need to spend it by the end of the year, most plans offer an online portal where you can review your balance, submit claims and check deadlines. The FSA administrator's information is typically listed on the back of your FSA card, Rouleau said.

articles.title: What midterm election blue wave rebuke of Trump means for renewable energy
articles.text:
As recently as 2022, many leaders in corporate America and the investment community were singing the praises of ESG — environmental, social, governance — as the foundation of stakeholder capitalism. It didn't take long for that tune to change, for understandable reasons.
President Trump didn't just make "ESG", "sustainability" and "climate change" dirty words in his "green new scam" rhetoric. The Trump administration's rollback of environmental regulations, elimination of clean energy subsidies and tax credits, defunding and halting of wind and solar projects, and embrace of the fossil fuels industry accelerated the backlash.
But renewable energy investing remains alive and well, notably among public and private funders of infrastructure projects and clean technology innovation. And following the midterm elections that gave climate-friendly Democrats control of the House and Senate, the prospects of reviving the clean energy agenda suddenly brightened.
Clean energy and solar stocks rallied the day after the election results, which "potentially reduces the risk of further political interference with renewable energy incentives and provides greater protection for the long-term economics of U.S. wind, solar and battery storage investments," Barclays analysts led by Peter Crampton wrote in a note.
While Trump can veto legislation to restore subsidies and credits and revive projects, and continue to issue executive orders on energy policy, some Republicans may be more inclined to help Democrats override the president in order to appeal to voters outraged over high energy prices — a sentiment expressed in the passage of multiple state initiatives to impede the build-out of electricity-hungry data centers.
The blue wave also shines a spotlight on a bipartisan permitting-reform bill awaiting Senate approval. Several progressive Democrats want to put off the vote until the new Congress convenes in January, giving them time to rewrite provisions favoring renewables projects over fossil fuel ventures.
Ultimately, the midterms could improve the outlook for investors focused on clean energy. That is likely to start with impact investors who specifically seek to generate a competitive financial rate of return alongside positive, proactive social and environmental impact. Opportunities can be found through public equity investments like mutual funds and ETFs that are constructed to invest in clean energy companies. But many investors also seek out pure-play clean energy positions offered through fixed income, private equity, private credit, venture capital, real assets and community-focused investments.
"There are many different approaches that could lead impact investors to be thinking about clean energy investments," said Amit Bouri, who's retiring as CEO of the Global Impact Investing Network at year's end. GIIN's 2026 survey of impact investors found that 56% have funds invested in clean energy and 25% plan to increase those investments over the next five years. The survey was conducted prior to the midterms.
"Clean energy infrastructure can be really compelling from an investment standpoint, because the financial thesis and impact thesis are mutually reinforcing," said Justina Lai, chief impact officer at LNW, a wealth management advisory firm. LNW has about $3.5 billion of its total $12.1 billion assets under management invested in impact strategies. She added that it's challenging to break down the number of clients who are specifically focused on clean energy and clean tech. "Climate change or climate action writ large is likely the most common impact priority that we encounter with our clients," she said.
While it might be hard to focus on the potential in the renewable energy sector in 2026 with energy commodities leading all sectors of the market as crude oil prices surged, some of the factors Lai cites should be on the radar of investors beyond the impact investing space.
She pointed to the nation's growing electricity demand — partly tied to data centers — its aging and constrained grid infrastructure, the increasing need for energy storage, the effects of geopolitics on energy security and rising energy costs as major factors driving clean energy investing. Simultaneously, though, because of declining costs and continuing maturity of many clean technologies, "we know that renewables are the lowest cost form of new-build generation, even on a fully unsubsidized basis," she said.
The proof is in the gigawatts. The U.S. is on pace to add a record 89 GW of clean energy capacity by the end of 2026, with installations projected to exceed that level in 2027, according to BloombergNEF's latest US Clean Energy Market Outlook. In just the first half of this year, the Environmental Defense Fund and Atlas Public Policy recently reported, 11.5 GW of solar, 8.3 GW of battery storage and 6.3 GW of wind power were installed.
U.S. investment in clean energy and transportation alone totaled $75 billion in the second quarter of 2026, the second-highest quarterly figure on record and up 22% from the previous quarter, according to the Clean Investment Monitor, a joint project of Rhodium Group and MIT's Center for Energy and Environmental Policy Research.
The supply chain has amped up, too.
