articles.title: These five stock groups could rally after Democrats' midterms sweep, analysts say
articles.text: Democrats swept in the U.S. midterm elections this week, and that could be a boon for several groups of stocks, according to Wall Street analysts. On Tuesday, Democrats flipped seven Senate and more than 40 House seats, giving the left-leaning party majority representation in Congress. That means Democrats will have greater say over legislative priorities on Capitol Hill — a power that has big implications for companies and their stocks. Stocks were volatile in the trading sessions following Election Day. The S & P 500 finished the week down 2.7%. Tech stocks got hit particularly hard, with the Nasdaq Composite falling 3.4% during the same period. The 30-stock Dow Jones Industrial Average fared better, only sliding 0.9% during the week. However, Wall Street has identified some potential winners amid the churn. A blue tsunami could bolster U.S. solar, airline and healthcare stocks, among others, several analysts said in notes to clients. Here are a few stocks they highlighted. Drone-related stocks With more Democrats soon to be in power, drone makers and drone battery manufacturers are likely to see their shares trade higher, according to William Blair. The investment firm noted that Democrats have stated their intention to lend more support to Ukraine in its war against Russia, which could lead to more money flowing to companies that make drones and the parts that power them. AMPX 3M mountain Amprius Technologies stock over the past three months One such firm that stands to benefit is drone battery manufacturer, Amprius Technologies , per William Blair. Roughly 50% of the company's revenue has been directly tied to Ukraine or to allies supporting the effort in 2026, according to the investment firm. "We view Amprius as a midterm winner as the 'blue wave' brings more support for Ukraine, a large driver of Amprius's demand," analyst Mark Shooter said Friday. "The midterm outcome could reverse the U.S. position from decreasing to increasing Ukraine funding, de-risk demand from this conflict, and offer expansion to Amprius revenues in 2027." Shooter has an outperform rating on Amprius. The stock has pulled back more than 22% over the past three months, but added 1.5% this week. Clean energy stocks Renewable energy firms, which generate energy via solar, wind or hydro power, could get a boost following the midterm elections, according to several industry analysts. "Some smaller policy tailwinds are possible: Congress is still considering a permitting reform bill ... [which has been] flagged as benefiting clean energy and geothermal," Wolfe Research analyst Tobin Marcus said Thursday. "And some incoming governors are proposing renewable mandates for data center power." FSLR 3M mountain First Solar performance over the past three months One stock that stands out is First Solar , according to William Blair. "Democrats swept the midterms, winning both chambers of Congress and flipping five governorships in Texas, Georgia, Ohio, Iowa and Nevada, as of the time of writing," analyst Jed Dorsheimer wrote in a Thursday note to clients. "Ultimately, we believe this will unlock support at a local level for more utility-scale solar procurement and siting." The Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act , which aims to expedite federal permit issuances to solar projects and expand grid development, is likely to become law with Democrats in power, the analyst added. Dorsheimer upgraded First Solar to outperform from market perform. Shares of the solar panel maker were up 15% over the past week, though the stock is down 23% so far in 2026. Healthcare Healthcare stocks are also poised to benefit from Democrats' congressional gains. Making medical care accessible is a major aim of the political party's agenda, which bodes well for some healthcare stocks, according to Wolfe Research. "Presumptive Speaker Jeffries has explicitly indicated that [lawmakers'] 'first 100 hours' agenda will include fully repealing the Medicaid cuts … and restoring the expanded [Affordable Care Act] premium tax credits that expired at the end of 2025," Wolfe's Marcus wrote Thursday. "So it makes perfect sense for investors to be focused on healthcare after the blue wave." The analyst noted that the potential tailwinds could be greatest for hospitals, although it could take "quite a while" for those to materialize. Shares of hospital operators HCA Healthcare and Universal Health Services have popped 4.6% and 11.1%, respectively, since the beginning of this week. More broadly, healthcare stocks have surged as of late. The Vanguard Health Care Index Fund ETF (VHT) has climbed more than 10% over the past three months as investors have rotated out of technology stocks and embraced more defensive plays due to credit risks tied to the ongoing artificial intelligence buildout. Airline stocks Airline stocks could rally following a big blue sweep this election season, according to Citigroup. "Investors … may be missing the effect that a dramatic increase in consumer sentiment among Democrats in the wake of the midterms could have on consumer discretionary demand, such as air travel," Citigroup analyst John Godyn said Wednesday in a note to clients. "As long as Republican consumer sentiment does not collapse 1:1 with any improvement in Democrat consumer sentiment (and implicitly assuming that Democrats and Republicans travel roughly a similar amount per capita), one could argue that the midterms may give airlines a boost in demand." The U.S. Global Jets ETF (JETS) , which invests in U.S. and international airlines, has risen about 2% since Election Day. Delta Air Lines and United Airlines led gains among airlines this past week, jumping 8.8% and 8.2%, respectively. Specialty REITs A few specialty Real Estate Investment Trusts are likely to rally, according to Barclays. "Voters largely favored candidates and ballot measures that oppose data center development … [which] could slow the pace of industry-wide construction," analyst Brendan Lynch said Wednesday in a note to clients. "We view our coverage as net beneficiaries from the pricing power that limitations on construction will create." Lynch pointed to Equinix , Iron Mountain and Digital Realty Trust as three potential beneficiaries of that shift. "Our sense is that EQIX and IRM's pipelines are essentially fully approved, and DLR faces only limited permitting risk for projects that would commence years from now," the analyst wrote. Those three REITs have fallen between 4% and 13% over the past three months, largely due to rising interest rates that have diminished the appeal of some dividends and lowered property valuations. However, the pullback offers a good opportunity to scoop up shares, according to Barclays.

articles.title: Berkshire shares surge as Wall Street swoons amid AI fears
articles.text:
(This is the Warren Buffett Watch newsletter, news and analysis on all things Warren Buffett and Berkshire Hathaway. You can sign up here to receive it every Friday evening in your inbox.)
Berkshire shares surge as Wall Street swoons amid AI fears
Berkshire Hathaway shares roared past the S&P 500 index this week as investors moved money away from slumping tech stocks and moved into what appears to be the relative safety of a traditional conglomerate with relatively little exposure to artificial intelligence amid fears massive spending on data centers won't pay off.
One month ago, Berkshire's widely held B shares were underperforming the S&P by 13.6 percentage points for the year.
With help from three more record-high closes this week, Berkshire is now 5.8 percentage points ahead of the benchmark.
Berkshire more than doubled its share repurchases last quarter to $9.6 billion, while operating earnings declined slightly, the company said on Saturday.
Berkshire was up more than 5% this week while the S&P fell almost 2.7%.
The contrast is even sharper with the Nasdaq Composite, which fell 3.4% on the week.
Thursday's especially heavy tech selling pushed the index down more than 10% below its most recent high in what is commonly referred to as a "correction," but it did make up some of its lost ground Friday.
Two weeks ago, Berkshire's share prices completely erased all of the roughly 15% drop they suffered in the three months following Warren Buffett's surprise announcement at the 2025 shareholders meeting that he would step down as CEO at the end of that year.
Now they are up 6% from the record high closes they hit the Friday before Buffett's revelation on May 3, 2025.
Alphabet's slide cited as example of 'disappointing' stock picks
Berkshire is not completely removed from the convulsions around AI.
Abel told us in early September he sees a "significant opportunity" ahead for Berkshire Hathaway Energy to provide electricity to data centers.
He also expected Berkshire would benefit from its big bet on Google parent Alphabet, saying he and Warren Buffett knew AI was "going to have a significant impact on America and businesses," and "we saw Google as a significant player."
Now that investment is getting negative reviews this week as the stock slumps along with other companies related to AI.
As of the end of June, Berkshire reported it owned almost 106 million shares of Alphabet, including 28.6 million shares it bought directly from the company in June: $5 billion of its Class A shares (GOOGL) for $351.81 each and another $5 billion of Class C shares (GOOG) for $348.20 each.
They are around $284 per share now.
It bought another $7 billion of Alphabet shares on the open market during the second quarter, adding to the position it started building in last year's third quarter, an investment initiated by Warren Buffett.
Bloomberg suggests that "with cracks in the AI trade starting to show, Berkshire's sudden push [into AI] may appear ill-timed."
On June 30, the position had a market value of $37.8 billion and it was the third largest equity holding in Berkshire's portfolio.
Since then both the Class A and Class C shares have dropped by around 20% and the stake is now valued at $30.2 billion, falling behind Coca-Cola's $38.3 billion to the portfolio's #4 position.
(In just over a week, we'll find out whether Berkshire made any changes to its Alphabet position during the third quarter ending September 30.)
Bloomberg quotes CFRA Research analyst Cathy Seifert as saying, "I do think that part of this may be a conscious decision to increase their exposure. One has to ask the question though, is it a little late?"
But the article notes that "for dedicated value investors and longtime Berkshire observers, such jitters may not really matter," with Keefe Bruyette & Woods analyst Meyer Shields saying Abel probably sees bets on AI as a long-term wager on the technology's potential, in keeping with the "conservatism that you would expect at Berkshire Hathaway."
At Barron's, however, Andrew Bary sees what he estimates is a $3 billion loss on Alphabet as part of a "disappointing" long-term trend in Berkshire's stock choices
"The company hasn't created much value from stock picking during the current decade" even though the "S&P 500 has returned 150% since the end of 2019 and tech stocks have quadrupled."
While Berkshire's investments in five Japanese "trading houses," Chevron, and Chubb have done well, "there have been plenty of losers or simply mediocre investments that have been closed out."
He cites Verizon, HP, Paramount (now Skydance), General Motors, Constellation Brands, and Pool.
While he estimates Berkshire's Occidental Petroleum investment is up about 20% from what it paid, OXY is "far behind most energy stocks" amid this year's big increase in crude prices.
Bary also lists stocks that have continued to rise in price after Berkshire cut its stakes, with Apple being the worst offender.
That stake has been reduced by 75% since 2023 at what Bary calculates is an average selling price around $200 per share, well below AAPL's current $342.
Despite those sales, Apple is Berkshire's largest equity holding with a market value of $78 billion. The stock is up 1200% since Berkshire started buying it at the beginning of 2016, at a time when many thought the company had already seen its best days.
Bary thinks Abel will probably keep Berkshire's core equity investments but may concentrate more on his strengths going forward: improving Berkshire's operating companies and making new acquisitions.
His conclusion: "Barring a market rout, equity investing may not be central to Berkshire anymore.
"And if any new Berkshire holdings are revealed soon, it may not be a good idea to buy them. The record hasn't been great."
Small buy helps lift Sirius XM shares
Berkshire Hathaway's disclosure that it had made a relatively small $27 million addition to its $4.1 billion Sirius XM position helped fuel an ongoing rally that lifted the satellite radio company's shares to a 52-week high this week.
On Thursday morning last week, Sirius XM reported a 14% increase in its Q3 free cash flow, 5,000 more self-pay subscribers, and it raised its 2026 full-year financial guidance.
The stock ended 4.9% higher that day at $28.67.
On Friday, Monday, and Tuesday, Berkshire bought more than 924 thousand shares at an average price of $29.10 as the stock continued to gain ground, ending Tuesday at $30.80.
Berkshire disclosed the buys late Tuesday evening, apparently helping to fuel an additional 8.4% gain as the stock closed at $33.40 on Wednesday.
It hit a 52-week intraday high of $33.76 on Thursday but finished lower Friday at $32.40.
Overall, Sirius XM is up 18.6% since the earnings release and has gained 62.0% so far this year.
It's the first addition to Berkshire's stake since late-July and early-August last year.
In 2025, it bought a total of 7.3 million shares at an average price of $21.86.
The position is likely one of portfolio manager Ted Weschler's stocks.
Berkshire utility asks for 57% rate hike in Northern California
Pacific Power, a unit of Berkshire Hathaway's PacifiCorp, is asking California regulators for a 57% rate increase that would raise the typical residential electric bill by $120 a month.
The Wall Street Journal calls it a "stunning request even in an era of rising electricity costs."
The utility says the hike would be partially offset by a 14% decrease taking effect on January 1.
A lot of the $103 million that would be generated by the increase is already being spent on efforts to make power equipment in the sparsely populated and heavily wooded area more resistant to wildfires.
The utility is facing around $637 million in liability claims for fires in 2020 and 2022.
This week, Reuters reports, Oregon's Supreme Court heard arguments on whether to revive a jury verdict that could expose PacifiCorp "to tens of billions of dollars of potential damages over its role in four Oregon wildfires in 2020."
BUFFETT & BERKSHIRE AROUND THE INTERNET
Some links may require a subscription:
HIGHLIGHTS FROM CNBC'S BUFFETT ARCHIVE
Work in the age of artificial intelligence (2017)
Warren Buffett and Charlie Munger share their opinions about how artificial intelligence could affect the economy, the government, and how much time people spend on leisure activities.
ANDREW ROSS SORKIN: Thomas Kimay (PH) is here. He's a 27-year-old shareholder from Kentfield, California.
And I should preface this question by saying that he was here 17 years ago at 10 years old, asked you a question from the audience asking you if the internet might hurt some of Berkshire's investments.
At the time, you said you wanted to see how things would play out. He's now updated the question. (Buffett laughs)
"What do you think about the implications of artificial intelligence on Berkshire's businesses, beyond autonomous driving and GEICO, which you've talked about already? ...
WARREN BUFFETT: I certainly have no special insights on artificial intelligence, but I will bet a lot of things happen in that field in the next couple of decades, and probably a shorter timeframe.
They should lead, I would certainly think — but again, I don't bring much to this party. But I would certainly think they would result in significantly less employment in certain areas.
But that's good for society.
And it may not be good for a given business, but let's take it to the extreme.
Let's assume one person could push a button and, essentially, through various machines and robotics, all kinds of things, turn out all of the output we have in this country.
So, everybody's — there's just as much output as we have. It's all being done by, you know, instead of 150-some million people being employed, one person.
You know, is the world better off or not?
Well, certainly we'd work a lot less hours a week — of work per week and so on.
I mean, it would be a good thing, but it would require enormous transformation in how people relate to each other, what they expect of government, you know, all kinds of things. And, of course, as a practical matter, more than one person would keep working.
But pushing the idea that way is one of the — you'd certainly think that's one of the consequences of making great progress in artificial intelligence.
And that's enormously prosocial, eventually. It's enormously disruptive in other ways. And it can have huge problems, in terms of a democracy and how it reacts to that...
CHARLIE MUNGER: Well, you're painting a very funny world where everybody's engaged in trade. And the trade is, I give you golf lessons and you dye my hair. And that would be a world kind of like the royal family of Kuwait or something.
And I don't think it would be good for America to have everything produced by one person and the rest of us just engaged in leisure.

articles.title: Tech companies face mounting child safety lawsuits while pushing AI into schools
articles.text:
Tech companies have spent years telling parents they're working to make their products safer for children. But ongoing jury trials, settlements and related litigation against the likes of Meta, Google and Snap suggest that they're not doing enough.
The latest examples landed this week. Snap confidentially settled a case claiming that its technology caused severe psychological distress to two teenage users. Meta, TikTok and YouTube previously settled with the plaintiffs in the same suit. And Google was sued this week by the parents of a child who allegedly suffered a psychological crisis after chatting with the Gemini AI chatbot in Google Classroom.
Concern is intensifying as artificial intelligence companies pursue trillion-dollar valuations, and established internet giants pour money into developing advanced AI models while pushing them into the classroom. Products and features intended to maximize engagement can have detrimental effects on users, thus warranting "broader systemic changes in tech design, particularly when children are using them," said developmental psychologist Kate Blocker.
"I think it's so so important that children's safety is being considered when these products — AI, social media, et cetera — are being designed, and not after the fact as these problems emerge," said Blocker, the director of research and programs for the nonprofit Children and Screens.
Snap's settlement this week, which spared CEO Evan Spiegel from testifying in a Los Angeles court, continues a general trend of tech companies attempting to shield themselves from public scrutiny due to the various high-profile child-safety related trials this year, said Joseph McNally, the director of emerging litigation at McNicholas & McNicholas.
The case was one of several lawsuits related to the social media personal injury trial that Meta and YouTube lost earlier this year. More trials are slated to commence in March.
"I view this settlement and the other settlements in this space as an effort by tech companies to turn a corner, not only because I think that there were real legal challenges, but also the reputation of their products, the reputation of their companies has really been hit," said McNally, a former acting U.S. attorney for the Central District of California.
"The parties are pleased to have been able to resolve this matter in an amicable manner," a Snap spokesperson said in a statement.
"We've built safeguards, launched safety tutorials, and partnered with experts and because safety is never finished, we remain committed to continually strengthening the safety, privacy, and well-being of our community," the Snap spokesperson said.
But there remains a federal case involving Meta, TikTok, Snap and YouTube and a litany of nationwide school districts, along with various state attorneys general suits. In August, Meta agreed to pay nearly $17 billion to settle with a group of state AGs in a child mental health case. Some AGs are still pursuing similar suits against Meta's rivals.
The social media lawsuits have helped inform parents and the public about how the industry designs products used by teenagers and children, McNally said.
"It's the technology arms race that continues," he said. "What is oftentimes missing is how you balance that participation in the arms race with utility and then product safety."
More scrutiny in the classroom
Google ran into more criticism this week for moving too fast. The New York Times reported on Tuesday that K-12 schools that don't allow use of Google's AI tools for students will lose access to search. Chris Phillips, vice president for education at Google, told the Times that, "Search and AI are deeply integrated."
That coincided with the new lawsuit against Google centering on a teen's alleged suicidal crisis that the parents attributed to the company's Gemini AI. The plaintiff's attorneys allege that "despite Gemini's known risks, Google hastily integrated" Gemini into Chromebook computers for school children.
"We are reviewing the claims in the lawsuit and we take this very seriously," a Google spokesperson said in a statement. "We've worked extensively with medical professionals and academic experts to build features that help young people find critical support and trusted resources when they need it."
Google and its internet peers have for decades been able to rely on Section 230.
Passed in 1996, the federal legislation has protected social media companies from being sued over content posted by their users. That's why plaintiffs' attorneys and state AGs have been focused on alleged harms stemming from the design of the tech platforms as opposed to their content.
Some plaintiffs are using the same tactics against AI companies. OpenAI faces several lawsuits from state AGs and plaintiff attorneys, taking cues from the social media suits in alleging that the design of ChatGPT can pose risks to children.
The litigation could become a growing financial risk as the company plans for a potential blockbuster IPO. OpenAI competitor Anthropic, which is planning to go public this month, highlighted the issue in its prospectus, even though the Claude creator prohibits children from using its product.
"This is a clear indication that tech companies anticipate more litigation risks than they did a decade ago," said Michele Neitz, a professor at the University of San Francisco School of Law.
Blocker said that the highly personalized nature of current AI-powered chat apps makes it "a little bit unpredictable" to determine exactly what the apps will say to kids. She stressed the importance of testing and evaluating these products for children's developmental safety from the start, "not after harms start happening."
This collective litigation has helped educate the public on the potential pitfalls of poor product design choices, Blocker said. And it could be a catalyzing force for change in the tech industry.
"Certainly there's a hope that this will motivate real systemic change, both from a regulation standpoint and internal company decision-making standpoint," Blocker said.
If you are having suicidal thoughts or are in distress, contact the Suicide & Crisis Lifeline at 988 for support and assistance from a trained counselor.

articles.title: Trump says U.S. carried out ‘minor strikes’ on Iran as missiles hit Qeshm Island
articles.text:
President Donald Trump told reporters Friday that the U.S. carried out "minor strikes" on Iran, amid reports that two missiles struck Qeshm Island near the Strait of Hormuz.
The missiles struck the island on Friday, Iranian news agency Tasnim reported, according to Reuters. Tasnim said there was no official information on damage, Reuters added.
The island lies off Iran's southern coast, near the Strait of Hormuz, the vital artery for oil and gas that has become a flashpoint in the war.
Speaking to reporters Friday evening after landing in West Palm Beach, Florida, Trump didn't comment specifically on Qeshm Island, saying: "I don't want to talk about it."
But he added: "We do minor strikes, but they knock out. They built a little bit of an anti-aircraft device, and we knocked it out in about 15 minutes, maybe five." He did not explicitly confirm that he was referring to the reported strikes on Qeshm.
The strikes are the first since Tuesday's midterm elections, after analysts and regional officials had debated whether the vote would lead Trump toward further escalation or renewed diplomacy.
The U.S. struck the same island Monday, in what a U.S. official told MS Now was a "defensive measure."
'They want to make a deal very badly'
Trump also told reporters Friday that Iran wants "to make a deal very badly. They have 300% inflation. Their navy's gone. Their airport, everything's gone, and they want to make a deal."
The International Monetary Fund forecast that Iran's consumer prices would rise by an average of 78.6% in 2026, in a report published Oct. 13.
When asked if he wanted to make a deal "really soon," Trump said: "Well, we have nobody getting hurt, nobody getting killed.
"You know, this is a war that we may have been there for seven months, but we probably fought for three or four weeks, really fought. And again, you look at World War One; that's a war. World War Two; that's a war."
Iran has said it wants more than "paper commitments" from the U.S. before entering a new phase of diplomatic talks.
"We must see practical measures by the Americans," Ali Bagheri Kani, deputy secretary of Iran's Supreme National Security Council, told state broadcaster IRIB on Friday, according to Press TV.

articles.title: The race is on to build the first fusion power plant — and Europe is looking to Japan for help
articles.text:
The race is on to build the world's first commercial fusion power plant — and one of Europe's leading contenders in the field has just received a boost.
Munich-based Proxima Fusion signed memoranda of understanding with two Japanese industrial partners, Fujikura and Kyoto Fusioneering, in Tokyo on Oct. 28. Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi and German Chancellor Friedrich Merz — who was visiting in a bid to deepen trade ties — were both in attendance.
Ann Mettler, president of Catalyse Europe, a Brussels-based clean-energy think tank, and a former vice president of Breakthrough Energy, said developing the technology should be a strategic imperative for Europe.
"Europe is a resource-poor geography and we are very dependent on China. The world is in competition for technological supremacy — this is a zero-sum game," Mettler told CNBC, speaking in a personal capacity.
"Fusion is a silver bullet because the promise is abundant, clean, limitless energy."
Fusion energy seeks to replicate the way the sun produces power, using super-heated plasma to fuse two light atomic nuclei into one heavier one, releasing vast amounts of energy in the process.
There are two main approaches: one uses high-powered lasers, while the other uses powerful magnets to confine the plasma. Proxima is developing a type of magnetic device called a stellarator, which is designed to hold the plasma in place for long periods.
The agreement with Kyoto Fusioneering will expand existing work on next-generation gyrotrons — devices that generate high-power microwaves used to heat the plasma.
Why HTS tape matters
Proxima's agreement with 141-year-old Fujikura will explore plans for industrial-scale manufacturing in Germany of high-temperature superconducting, or HTS, tape, a specialized metallic tape that is superconducting at relatively high temperatures and can carry electrical current with virtually no resistive losses.
The tape is wound into coils to form powerful magnets that confine and control the heated plasma inside the stellarator.
Francesco Sciortino, CEO and co-founder of Proxima Fusion, told CNBC that Fujikura, which employs over 50,000 people worldwide, was a leader in manufacturing high-temperature superconductors, having built its reputation in optical fibers. "They think this tape has the potential to be the next optical fibre," he said.
He said Proxima, which is studying plans to build a manufacturing facility in Lower Saxony, hoped to make around 5,000 kilometers, or 3,100 miles, of tape annually by 2030.
The 140 million euro ($160 million) facility would be financed partly by the proceeds of a $468 million funding round in July, which valued Proxima, whose backers include Alphabet-owned Google, at $2.7 billion.
Proxima expects to need around 20,000 kilometers (12,400 miles) of the tape for its "Alpha" fusion demonstrator and a further 40,000 kilometers (24,900 miles) for its planned "Stellaris" fusion power station.
Europe’s fusion supply chain
Sciortino said that establishing production of the tape in Germany was crucial as it would help Europe create the expertise and supply chains needed to turn its fusion research leadership into industrial capability.
This is where Europe has historically struggled, according to Catalyse Europe's Mettler.
If Europe is first to develop this technology, it will give us a huge advantage, but key to that will be building the supply chainAnn MettlerCatalyse Europe
"Every geography wants to turn leadership in science into industrial leadership and this is where Europe has traditionally been not so good — turning that scientific leadership into euros," she said.
While Europe had industrial giants to be proud of, disruptors tended to be more successful in frontier technologies, according to Mettler.
"If Europe is first to develop this technology, it will give us a huge advantage, but key to that will be building the supply chain," she said.
Commercial fusion competitors
Sciortino said he remains confident Proxima will be the first company to turn on a pilot plant — but stressed the key to profitability would be making that plant as simple as possible to operate.
"You can have complexity in the design, manufacturing and operation of the plant," he said. "We can take care of the complexity in the design and manufacturing, but our view is that there needs to be simplicity in the operation. We are aiming for net energy gain during the early 2030s."
But Proxima has some well-heeled competitors. They include U.S.-based Commonwealth Fusion Systems, which is also backed by Google, and Helion Energy, as well as Canada's General Fusion. China has a number of state-backed players, most notably China Fusion Energy Co., while Tokyo-based Helical Fusion leads Japan's push.
"The supply chain in fusion energy needs to be built years before — people often think of frontier technologies as a switch that can be thrown," Mettler said. "That is not the case here."

articles.title: Bức thư tay gây sốt cộng đồng mạng của giám đốc sở ở Điện Biên
articles.text:
Bức thư tay gây sốt cộng đồng mạng của giám đốc sở ở Điện Biên
Những ngày qua, bức thư viết tay của Trần Hải Hà, Giám đốc Sở Văn hóa, Thể thao và Du lịch tỉnh Điện Biên mời các runner tham gia giải chạy gây xôn xao mạng xã hội. Trong thời kỳ bùng nổ của công nghệ số và AI, bức thư tay truyền thống tạo ra hiệu ứng truyền thông bất ngờ.
Bức thư tay đóng dấu đỏ của Giám đốc Sở Văn hóa Thể thao và Du lịch
Lá thư mời dài ba trang viết tay của ông Trần Hải Hà được chia sẻ trên mạng xã hội, thu hút sự quan tâm của cộng đồng mạng nói chung và cộng đồng chạy bộ nói riêng.
Trong thư, Giám đốc Sở Văn hóa, Thể thao và Du lịch tỉnh Điện Biên gửi lời mời các câu lạc bộ, hội, nhóm và vận động viên trên cả nước tham gia Giải chạy địa hình chinh phục đỉnh Pu Tó Cọ “Theo dấu chân Đại tướng” năm 2026.
Qua bức thư, ông Hà mong muốn người dân, du khách khi đến với Pu Tó Cọ không chỉ tham gia chạy bộ, leo núi mà còn có dịp tìm hiểu về lịch sử Mường Phăng, nơi Đại tướng Võ Nguyên Giáp và Bộ Chỉ huy chiến dịch Điện Biên Phủ đưa ra những quyết định lịch sử. Ông viết rằng, người tham gia giải chạy sẽ cảm nhận được giá trị của hòa bình, độc lập, tự do hôm nay và ý chí, nghị lực của dân tộc Việt Nam.
Chia sẻ với phóng viên Báo Tiền Phong về lá thư, ông Hà cho biết đã viết vào chiều 31/10, sau chuyến khảo sát thực địa cung đường chạy lên đỉnh Pu Tó Cọ vào buổi sáng. Những cảm xúc ngay sau chuyến đi giúp ông nhanh chóng hoàn thành lá thư. “Hôm ấy, tôi viết một mạch, trong một giờ, không tẩy xóa, không sai một từ nào”, ông Hà kể.
Trong thời kỳ mà đa số mọi người viết văn bản bằng máy tính, điện thoại, thậm chí là AI như hiện nay, việc ông Hà viết thư tay trở thành hiện tượng lạ. Lý giải điều này, ông Hà nói: “Tôi nghĩ đơn giản rằng, đây là cách thể hiện sự trân trọng".
Ông Hà cho biết, trong công việc hằng ngày, dù phần lớn hoạt động xử lý, trao đổi công việc và hội họp hiện được thực hiện qua máy tính, thiết bị điện tử nhưng bản thân ông cùng nhiều cộng sự vẫn duy trì thói quen ghi chép, phác thảo ý tưởng, viết ý kiến và ghi chú bằng giấy, bút.
Tất nhiên, bức thư nêu trên của ông Hà vẫn vì mục tiêu công việc, là hoạt động thực thi công vụ nên được ký tên, đóng dấu, thậm chí đóng cả dấu giáp lai, có giá trị như một văn bản của cơ quan Nhà nước.
Theo ông Hà, Điện Biên là tỉnh miền núi, biên giới còn nhiều khó khăn. Vì vậy, việc tổ chức giải cũng là cơ hội quảng bá hình ảnh vùng đất, con người, thu hút khách du lịch, góp phần tạo sinh kế và tăng thêm thu nhập cho người dân địa phương.
Bức thư sau đó được đăng trên Fanpage trên Facebook của Sở Văn hóa, Thể thao và Du lịch tỉnh Điện Biên, lập tức nhận được hàng trăm lượt like, thả tim, chia sẻ và bình luận.
"Có những điều tưởng chừng rất nhỏ nhưng lại thể hiện sự tâm huyết và trách nhiệm của người đứng đầu", một tài khoản comment. Một tài khoản khác bình luận: "Rất trân trọng hình ảnh Giám đốc Sở tự tay viết những bức thư mời tham gia Giải chạy Pú Tó Cọ. Một cách làm giản dị, chân thành nhưng chứa đựng sự trân trọng đối với từng cá nhân, đơn vị và mong muốn lan tỏa những giá trị tốt đẹp của thể thao, văn hóa, du lịch Điện Biên".
Sau những lời khen, nhiều người đã lập tức hưởng ứng, đăng ký tham gia giải chạy. "Với bức thư mời đầy tâm huyết và sự trân trọng ntn chắc sẽ khó có runner nào có thể chối từ! Chúc giải chạy thành công rực rỡ!", một tài khoản chia sẻ.
Giám đốc không ngại làm MC
Không chỉ tự mình viết thư mời gọi runner và du khách đến với Điện Biên, ông Trần Hải Hà cũng từng trực tiếp tham gia nhiều hoạt động quảng bá văn hóa, du lịch của tỉnh.
Trên Fanpage của sở Văn hoá Thể thao và Du lịch tỉnh Điện Biên hay kênh TikTok “Điện Biên Ngày Mới”..., từ khi còn là Phó Giám đốc Sở, ông Hà đã xuất hiện trong nhiều video với vai trò người dẫn, giới thiệu các điểm đến, sự kiện văn hóa, du lịch của địa phương.
Hình ảnh vị Phó Giám đốc, nay là Giám đốc Sở Văn hoá Thể thao và Du lịch Điện Biên với phong thái trẻ trung, dẫn chuyện tung tẩy đã thu hút không ít người xem. Trong đó, video ông Hà giới thiệu các chương trình du lịch Tết 2026 của Điện Biên trên Fanpage của Sở đã đạt hơn 155 nghìn lượt xem; video ông giới thiệu Lễ hội Ném còn ba nước Việt Nam - Lào - Trung Quốc, thu hút hơn 100 nghìn lượt xem trên kênh TikTok “Điện Biên Ngày Mới”.
Theo ông Hà, đây là cách làm mới trong công tác tuyên truyền, đưa thông tin chính thống đến gần hơn với công chúng, đặc biệt là giới trẻ, thông qua những nội dung ngắn gọn, sinh động trên nền tảng số.
Cùng ông Hà, các lãnh đạo phòng ban, trung tâm của Sở cũng "lên hình" để quảng bá du lịch Điện Biên. Ông Hà cho hay, việc cán bộ, công chức trực tiếp tham gia sáng tạo nội dung cũng giúp thông tin được truyền tải gần gũi hơn, đồng thời khuyến khích người dân, du khách cùng quảng bá, kể những câu chuyện về Điện Biên.
Giải leo núi chinh phục đỉnh Pu Tó Cọ tại xã Mường Phăng lần đầu tiên được tổ chức Tháng 12/2025. Năm 2026 là lần thứ hai giải được tổ chức, với tên gọi Giải chạy địa hình chinh phục đỉnh Pu Tó Cọ “Theo dấu chân Đại tướng”.
Giải chạy năm nay được tổ chức ngày 28/11 với ba cự ly 6km, 16km và 26km. Cung đường đưa vận động viên đến với đỉnh Pu Tó Cọ, nơi hơn 70 năm trước từng là đài quan sát của quân đội ta. Khu vực này gắn với Di tích Sở Chỉ huy Chiến dịch Điện Biên Phủ, nơi Đại tướng Võ Nguyên Giáp cùng Bộ chỉ huy chiến dịch đưa ra những quyết định lịch sử, góp phần làm nên chiến thắng Điện Biên Phủ. Ngoài chạy bộ, vận động viên còn có cơ hội tham quan các thắng cảnh, di tích lịch sử, thưởng thức đặc sản Điện Biên và xem biểu diễn văn nghệ.
Bên cạnh giải chạy địa hình nêu trên, tỉnh Điện Biên đang cùng với Báo Tiền Phong triển khai giải chạy Tiền Phong Marathon - Điện Biên Discovery. Giải chạy sẽ diễn ra trong 3 ngày, từ 31/12/2026 đến 2/1/2027 tại tỉnh Điện Biên. Giải chạy hứa hẹn sẽ làm sống lại những bản hùng ca huyền thoại trên vùng đất Điện Biên đậm chất sử thi.
Tiền phong

articles.title: Máy bay nội địa Nga được trang bị nhiều công nghệ, nhưng có tiết kiệm nhiên liệu hơn đối thủ Airbus?
articles.text:
Máy bay nội địa Nga được trang bị nhiều công nghệ, nhưng có tiết kiệm nhiên liệu hơn đối thủ Airbus?
Dù đánh dấu bước tiến công nghệ vượt bậc của ngành hàng không Nga, dòng máy bay thương mại MS-21-310 vẫn đối mặt với thử thách không nhỏ khi đặt lên bàn cân so sánh về hiệu quả nhiên liệu với thế hệ Airbus Neo.
Động cơ PD-14 và bài toán chênh lệch công nghệ với LEAP-1A
Sự ra đời của động cơ PD-14 đại diện cho một bước nhảy vọt quan trọng đối với ngành chế tạo động cơ máy bay nội địa Nga. So với các thế hệ động cơ trước đây do Nga sản xuất, PD-14 vượt trội hơn hẳn về khả năng tiết kiệm nhiên liệu nhờ sở hữu kiến trúc hiện đại và thiết kế dạng mô-đun linh hoạt.
Tuy nhiên, khi đặt cạnh dòng động cơ LEAP-1A (do liên doanh CFM International của Mỹ và Pháp sản xuất) đang được trang bị trên dòng Airbus Neo, PD-14 vẫn bộc lộ những hạn chế nhất định về mặt giải pháp và vật liệu công nghệ.
Điểm khác biệt dễ nhận thấy nhất nằm ở tỷ số tách luồng. Trong khi LEAP-1A đạt tỷ lệ khoảng 11:1, thì thông số này trên PD-14 chỉ dừng lại ở mức 8,5:1. Tỷ số tách luồng càng cao đồng nghĩa với việc động cơ tối ưu hóa luồng không khí tốt hơn, từ đó làm giảm lượng tiêu hao nhiên liệu trên mỗi đơn vị lực đẩy.
Bên cạnh đó, LEAP-1A còn tích hợp nhiều vật liệu thế hệ mới như cánh quạt quạt hút bằng chất liệu composite và vật liệu composite gốc gốm ở khu vực tuabin áp suất thấp. Những giải pháp vật liệu tiên tiến này giúp giảm trọng lượng tổng thể và tăng độ bền nhiệt cho động cơ.
Mặc dù những yếu tố kỹ thuật này chưa thể lập tức quyết định mức chênh lệch tiêu thụ nhiên liệu chính xác trên từng chuyến bay cụ thể, chúng tạo ra một lợi thế không nhỏ về mặt hiệu suất vận hành dài hạn.
Trọng lượng tăng vọt và hệ quả thu hẹp tầm bay
Bên cạnh câu chuyện động cơ, chương trình nội địa hóa toàn bộ linh kiện trên MS-21-310 nhằm thay thế các phụ tùng nước ngoài cũng kéo theo những hệ lụy kỹ thuật rõ rệt. Việc loại bỏ các thiết bị nhập khẩu và thay bằng linh kiện sản xuất trong nước đã làm gia tăng đáng kể trọng lượng rỗng của tàu bay.
Sự gia tăng khối lượng này ảnh hưởng trực tiếp đến thông số tầm bay của chiếc máy bay. Theo tính toán công bố, tầm bay của MS-21-310 ở cấu hình 2 hạng ghế với sức chứa 175 hành khách đã bị sụt giảm từ 5.100 km xuống còn 3.830 km. Để so sánh, đối thủ Airbus A321neo hiện công bố tầm bay tối đa lên tới 7.400 km.
Dù tầm bay bị thu hẹp đáng kể, các chuyên gia tại tập đoàn chế tạo Yakovlev đánh giá con số 3.830 km vẫn hoàn toàn đủ khả năng đáp ứng nhu cầu thực tế. Thông số tầm bay hiện tại của MS-21-310 vẫn đảm bảo phục vụ trên 80% lượng hành khách luân chuyển nội địa Nga nếu tính từ trung tâm kết nối hàng không Moscow.
Điều này cho thấy chiếc máy bay vẫn hoàn toàn phù hợp với nhiệm vụ cốt lõi là duy trì mạng lưới giao thông hàng không trong nước.
Góc nhìn từ người trong cuộc và thách thức thương mại hóa
Trước những nghi ngại từ dư luận và giới phân tích, ông Anatoly Gaydansky - Phó Tổng giám đốc thứ nhất kiêm Giám đốc Trung tâm Kỹ thuật của PAO Yakovlev - đã thẳng thắn thừa nhận thực tế rằng các máy bay dòng Neo của Airbus có sự vượt trội hơn về hiệu quả nhiên liệu.
Ông Gaydansky nhấn mạnh: "Tất nhiên, các dòng máy bay lớp 'Neo' hiện nay có phần nhỉnh hơn chúng tôi về hiệu quả nhiên liệu. Tuy nhiên, mức độ vượt trội này hoàn toàn không mang tính thảm họa." Lãnh đạo Yakovlev khẳng định dù có khoảng cách, nhưng độ chênh lệch vẫn nằm trong biên độ chấp nhận được và không làm mất đi tính khả thi của dự án.
Đối với thị trường nội địa Nga, nhiệm vụ cấp bách nhất hiện nay không phải là đánh bại Airbus hay Boeing về mặt thông số, mà là nhanh chóng cung cấp lực lượng vận tải thay thế cho các dòng máy bay phương Tây đang dần rút khỏi khai thác. Ở khía cạnh này, MS-21-310 hoàn toàn có thể hoàn thành tốt vai trò của mình.
Tuy nhiên, câu chuyện sẽ phức tạp hơn nhiều nếu MS-21-310 tiến ra thị trường quốc tế. Tại đây, chiếc máy bay của Nga sẽ phải cạnh tranh trực tiếp với những dòng tàu bay đã khẳng định được tên tuổi.
Các hãng sản xuất phương Tây sở hữu lợi thế tuyệt đối về kinh nghiệm vận hành tích lũy qua nhiều thập kỷ, chuỗi cung ứng dịch vụ bảo dưỡng toàn cầu hoàn thiện và năng lực sản xuất quy mô lớn.
Sự chênh lệch về hiệu quả nhiên liệu giữa MS-21-310 và Airbus Neo là một thực tế kỹ thuật không thể phủ nhận. Tuy nhiên, trong bối cảnh chiến lược hiện tại, mục tiêu lớn nhất của chương trình MS-21-310 không chỉ dừng lại ở việc thu hẹp khoảng cách tiết kiệm nhiên liệu với các đối thủ phương Tây.
Bài toán quyết định sự thành bại của dự án trong thời gian tới nằm ở năng lực của Yakovlev trong việc thiết lập dây chuyền sản xuất hàng loạt ổn định, đồng thời xây dựng hệ thống hỗ trợ kỹ thuật và dịch vụ hậu mãi đủ mạnh để đáp ứng nhu cầu khai thác thực tế của các hãng hàng không.

articles.title: Why a wave of bomb threats is proving so difficult for Europe's aviation authorities to contain
articles.text:
A spate of bomb threats against passenger flights has forced diversions, emergency landings and military escorts across European airspace this week, stoking fear among passengers and heaping pressure on airlines.
Authorities have described the more than two dozen threats as malicious hoaxes, and no actual attacks have been carried out. But the incidents have highlighted the huge impact that even false claims can have on a tightly scheduled aviation network.
"This is really quite exceptional, I've never seen this before in my whole career," Wilfried Covent, head of security firm Covent Consulting with a specialization in aviation, told CNBC by phone.
"We've had bomb threats in flights and towards airports, but usually maybe a single copycat, one or two max. What we see now is a systematic attack on airlines and airports."
An email sent to European broadcasters on Friday claimed to be from the leader of the group behind the plane hoaxes and also said bombs had been placed in their buildings, prompting evacuations. No bombs were found at the sites.
"What happened this week is just a small part of what awaits Europe in the near future," the message said, according to Reuters.
The news agency said it could not verify the sender's identity, where the emails originated or whether they were linked to the threats against flights.
Covent said the "criminals" — who many security analysts say are likely to be state-backed actors working in coordination to disrupt public life for Europeans, but have not been identified — were well aware that the "weakest point of aviation is targeting it in-flight."
"With a threat on an airport or a general threat to aircraft, you can assess the situation without fully disrupting operations. When the threat is called on a specific flight number that is in the air, even with a hoax, that triggers international regulations which ensure you don't ignore it — it means a quick landing, evacuation and searches by specialist forces," he told CNBC.
"For the context of an assessment, you cannot say that 20 times before it has been a hoax so this time it is a hoax, the safety of passengers and crew is priority number one. The criminals know that."
Coordinated response
Responsibility for dealing with hoax attacks is split, international agencies told CNBC. Assessing security threats and implementing aviation security measures primarily falls to national authorities, working in coordination with airport operators, airlines and law enforcement.
Air traffic control will also be involved in finding aircraft with an appropriate place to land, while the European Union Aviation Safety Agency, or EASA and U.K.'s Civil Aviation Authority more broadly set aviation safety rules and set how airlines prepare their crews to respond to security threats. Within the European Union, the European Commission is involved in aviation security policy and coordination between member states.
The operational decisions also depend on where the threat arises. Joji Waites, director of flight safety, policy and regulation at the British Air Line Pilots Association, said airline assessors grade a threat as red, amber or green, but that an amber verdict would never be given if the plane is airborne.
If assessors judge a threat credible, the crew is informed and the captain takes command of decisions for the aircraft, guided by company procedures. On the ground, that may mean an evacuation, while in the air the priority is to land as soon and as safely as possible.
Read more
As well as the fear and disruption to specific flights, each diversion can then affect the next flight scheduled to use that aircraft, the crew's working hours and passengers with connections.
The network effect can be significant. Philip Baum, a visiting professor of aviation security at Coventry University, told AP that a single diversion could cost an airline as much as $250,000, including replacement crews, missed connections and disruption to the rest of the day's schedule.
"Diversions necessitated by these bomb threats are a disturbance to a system designed for predictability and efficiency, and lead to increased workload for pilots, Air Traffic Controllers and airports," an EASA spokesperson said in emailed comments.
"As these staff have all have been trained to cope with such unexpected developments, the immediate safety threat from individual hoax threats is low. However, the higher number of diversions places an additional strain on the system."
What can change?
National governments will already be looking at their aviation authority regulations and frameworks and there will be discussions at the European and global level, John Edwards, senior consultant at Gates Aviation in London, said by phone.
"Bomb threats to aviation have been going on for decades, what they'll need to be looking at is what's different. Why have there been so many, why have so many been considered sufficiently credible to warrant the kind of action that it's warranted?"
"There's a range of questions they should be able to work through fairly quickly to establish a broad-brush level of credibility. If there is some characteristic that is new, every time there is an event of this kind, it triggers a big collaboration to ensure recurrence is prevented going forward."
"In theory, he said, "the vast majority should be able to assessed and considered non-credible based on routine risk assessment processes and well established procedures."
However, Eric Schouten, a former intelligence liaison officer at the Dutch General Intelligence and Security Service and CEO of security consultancy Dyami, said that changes to existing procedural regulations would take some time and require balancing the views and responsibilities of countries, airports, safety authorities and the European Union, with geopolitics also playing a role.
"There is a high likelihood even more flights are going to be canceled or diverted. It's possible that next to be targeted could be railways and highways," he said.
"But they will figure it out. It's not the first time airlines have had to deal with hoax calls because there are always copycats."
"Whatever measures they come out with to address it, they won't share publicly" for risk of alerting the bad actors, he added.
Wilfried Covent said that while there would not be any quick changes to assessment protocol, "if this is really going on for ever and ever something will need to change or you'd have to stop flying completely."
"Based on what we've seen in the past with other kinds of threats, time goes on and the type of attack may change and move on," he continued, pointing to the wave of cyberattacks that has recently hit supermarket fridges and blood banks.
"As Europeans we need to be prepared."

articles.title: Thông qua đề án chuyển hơn 4.000 ha đất thuộc Phú Thọ về Hà Nội
articles.text:
Thông qua đề án chuyển hơn 4.000 ha đất thuộc Phú Thọ về Hà Nội
Chính phủ thông qua hồ sơ đề án điều chỉnh địa giới giữa Hà Nội và Phú Thọ, theo đó hơn 4.000 ha đất thuộc Phú Thọ dự kiến được chuyển về Hà Nội.
- 08-11-2026Đường tới sổ hồng chung cư Mường Thanh được “mở” bằng cơ chế sau hơn 10 năm chờ đợi
- 08-11-2026Đang vớt rác nhặt được túi tiền, hai công nhân tìm trả khách Nhật
- 08-11-2026Hà Nội chỉ đạo khẩn vụ thịt lợn nhũn bở 'do lợn stress' ở trường mầm non
Phó Thủ tướng Phạm Thị Thanh Trà vừa ký ban hành Nghị quyết 351 về hồ sơ Đề án điều chỉnh địa giới đơn vị hành chính giữa TP Hà Nội và tỉnh Phú Thọ .
Theo nghị quyết, Chính phủ quyết nghị thông qua hồ sơ đề án điều chỉnh địa giới đơn vị hành chính giữa Hà Nội và Phú Thọ theo đề nghị của Bộ Nội vụ.
Chính phủ giao Bộ Nội vụ chủ trì, phối hợp với các bộ, cơ quan liên quan tiếp thu đầy đủ ý kiến của các thành viên Chính phủ để hoàn thiện tờ trình, đề án, dự thảo nghị quyết của Quốc hội và dự thảo nghị quyết của Ủy ban Thường vụ Quốc hội về việc điều chỉnh địa giới giữa hai địa phương, cũng như điều chỉnh địa giới các đơn vị hành chính cấp xã có liên quan.
Bộ trưởng Bộ Nội vụ được giao thừa ủy quyền Thủ tướng, thay mặt Chính phủ ký tờ trình, đề án, báo cáo tiếp thu, giải trình và chỉnh lý hồ sơ theo ý kiến của Quốc hội, Ủy ban Thường vụ Quốc hội, các cơ quan của Quốc hội và đại biểu Quốc hội.
Bộ Nội vụ chịu trách nhiệm toàn diện về nội dung hồ sơ đề án, các dự thảo nghị quyết và những vấn đề đề xuất, báo cáo; chuẩn bị đầy đủ hồ sơ, tài liệu gửi Quốc hội, Ủy ban Thường vụ Quốc hội và các cơ quan của Quốc hội, bảo đảm chất lượng, thời hạn theo quy định.
Đồng thời, Bộ Nội vụ chủ động báo cáo, giải trình với Quốc hội, Ủy ban Thường vụ Quốc hội và kịp thời báo cáo Thủ tướng những vấn đề phát sinh vượt thẩm quyền.
Trước đó, chiều 28/10, HĐND TP Hà Nội thông qua Nghị quyết về việc cho ý kiến đối với đề án điều chỉnh địa giới đơn vị hành chính giữa Hà Nội và Phú Thọ.
Theo đó, HĐND TP Hà Nội tán thành phương án điều chỉnh 4.006,38 ha diện tích tự nhiên và 1.057 người (243 hộ) từ Phú Thọ về Hà Nội. Trong đó có 2.529,38 ha thuộc Vườn quốc gia Ba Vì và 1.477 ha vùng đệm.
Phạm vi điều chỉnh gồm 2.171,15 ha và 1.057 người thuộc xã Thịnh Minh, 742,32 ha thuộc xã Lương Sơn và 1.092,91 ha thuộc phường Kỳ Sơn, tỉnh Phú Thọ. Đồng thời, bổ sung 1.338 ha và 1.057 người vào xã Ba Vì, 2.668,38 ha vào xã Yên Xuân, Hà Nội.
Phần diện tích chuyển từ xã Lương Sơn và phường Kỳ Sơn, cũng như phần diện tích xã Thịnh Minh chuyển về xã Yên Xuân, không có dân cư thuộc phạm vi điều chỉnh.
Sáng 5/11, Quốc hội khóa XVI đồng ý bổ sung vào chương trình Kỳ họp thứ 2 việc xem xét điều chỉnh địa giới đơn vị hành chính giữa TP Hà Nội và tỉnh Phú Thọ.
